That this House condemns the government for having abandoned the population of Montreal through its obvious lack of political will to provide jobs and economic opportunities to the people of this region.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the motion before the House today, we are condemning the government for having abandoned the population of Montreal through its obvious lack of political will to provide jobs and economic opportunities to the people of this region.
Mr. Speaker, the unemployment rate in Montreal has now reached 13.1 percent, the highest municipal rate in Canada. Moreover, 22 percent of Montrealers are living in such poverty that the municipal rate in that regard is also the highest in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this motion may sound severe but it is not an exaggeration. Let me say this at the beginning: I do not want this debate to be a contest of rhetoric or a contest of partisan political verbiage. I am trying to make an honest attempt to examine a serious situation, to analyze its causes and to find solutions. I note that the first ones to laugh and make jokes about the resolution were members on the govemement side and I must say I am here today to let the facts speak for themselves.
If the government can put forward sound solutions, I would be the first to withdraw my motion of condemnation.
As I said at the beginning, Montreal has the highest urban unemployment rate in Canada. It has the highest urban poverty rate in Canada. Liberals did not create those facts or that situation. I am simply bringing it to the attention of the House as something that has to be dealt with.
There have been massive layoffs in Montreal, closures of factories and businesses, a high rate of bankruptcies. In Montreal at the present time there are over 188,000 individuals unemployed. Food banks are at their highest number and at their greatest demand. Last night I was at a meeting in my own constituency in Montreal, a district of Montreal that by some is considered a more prosperous area-which is not correct-but a report that I listened to last night with respect to the N.D.G. Food Depot showed that from 1990 to 1991 the increase in demand for persons served in that food bank went up by 218 per cent. In 1990 that food bank in N.D.G. served 7,600 persons and this year so far, 16,500 persons.
It has been estimated that in Montreal, there are
15,000	homeless people, people that are either sleeping on the street or sleeping in shelters, that have no home of their own.
I would like this debate to be a serious attempt to deal with a very sad and difficult situation. I want the facts to speak for themselves. Let me list the layoffs in Montreal which took place in 1990 and 1991.
I will only list those for the House that are over 100 persons: Valmet-Dominion in Lachine laid off 200; Black and Decker laid off 150; Marconi laid off 150; Bristol Myers Squibb in Candiac laid off 124; CBC laid off 160; Thibault in Pierreville laid off 150; General

Motors in Broisbriand laid off 1,700; Steinberg's laid off 150; Clairol in Knowlton, Quebec laid off 228; CN laid off 2,000 in the Montreal area; Miracle Food Mart, 350; Canadian Marconi, 13; Goodyear at Valleyfield, 890-
Is that in Montreal?

Yes. The hon. member says: Is that Montreal, too? It is in the region of Montreal. Mr. Speaker, here we have a minister of the Crown and a member of the government side making light of the fact that over 800 people are laid off at Valleyfield, which is in the Montreal region. As a matter of fact, not only is it in the Montreal region from a demographic point of view, but it is served by offices of this government from the Montreal area.
Rolland Inc., 293 laid off. That is in 1990. In 1991: Eaton's, 190 laid off; Noranda, 125; Culinar, 256; Circo Craft, 211; Pratt & Whitney, 1,200; Air Canada, 2,900 across the country but the head office is in Montreal and a large number of those will be in the Montreal area; Primo Foods, 194; Tele-Metropole, 200; Goodyear, 145; and of course one of the largest layoffs of all, Pascal's hardware, a company that was in business in Montreal for 87 years, just in the last month closed 21 stores and laid off 1,600; and today it was announced in the Montreal newspapers that Pratt & Whitney have announced a lay-off of another 200 by June 21, making the total lay-offs at Pratt & Whitney of 1,000.
There have been many reports on this situation in Montreal and again I emphasize to the government these reports speak for themselves. It is not the Liberals speaking. It is not the New Democrats speaking. These are reports commissioned by the province of Quebec, the city of Montreal, and other social agencies in Montreal which state the facts with respect to the city.
There is a report by /'Office de planification et de developpement du Quebec from March 1991, indicating
188,000	Montrealers out of work by the end of 1990 and a report of May 1990 by Centraide de Montreal which shows deepening poverty and an expanding underclass of Montrealers without jobs, with substandard housing, and with poor health.
This report was completed by a 14-member committee headed by Paul Lacoste, former rector of the Universite de Montreal. Its recommendations included protection for low-income individuals, equitable taxation, home nursing and care for the aged and handicapped, subsidized housing, massive training and literacy programs and incentives for employment. That is a report, I would like the government to note, not by Liberals or by opposition members but by a very responsible committee in Montreal.
The 1989 report by federal economist, Mr. Jules Leger, stated that the large number of low income families puts Montreal in the forefront in terms of poor compared to other areas of Canada. Montreal, he said, has 192,000 more poor people than all of the four Atlantic provinces.
In April 1990, le Regroupement des departements de sante communautaire du Montreal Metropolitan stated that one in four Montreal residents live below the poverty line. In May 1990, a report by the Ministere des Affaires sociales du Quebec warned that Montreal is becoming impoverished faster than the rest of the province. The Canadian Apparel Manufacturers Institute expects the free trade agreement to kill fully one-third of 40,000 jobs in the Montreal region by the year 2000.
Finally, we have the Picard report from a commission which was appointed by this Conservative government to put forward a plan of action for Montreal to reinvigorate the city's economy and to create jobs. I will deal more with that report in a few minutes but that report made 84 recommendations, hardly any of which have been taken up by the government.
I would like to refer to a few of the clippings that have been put forward describing the situation in Montreal.
Bankruptcy jumped by 50 per cent in Quebec. Of course, a great majority of the businesses in Quebec are in Montreal.
Another clipping from April 1990 reads: "City Facing Unemployment Crisis, the Trade Unions Say in Montreal". Michel Bruillet, spokesman for Comite Regional de Syndicat de Montreal told reporters that there were
188,000	people without work in the Montreal employment pool.
He said action must be taken to deal with this very serious problem.
An article from the Southam newspapers of February 16, 1991: "Quebec Manufacturers Among the Hardest Hit Victims of the Free Trade Agreement."
An article from La Presse, December 1990: [Translation]
"The level of activity in the manufacturing sector will decline unless there is a radical change in attitude". This is from the Montreal Board of Trade.

"Economic Outlook Worsens: A Report by the Conseil de Patrons du Quebec."
It goes on and on.
Another report was by Secor, an agency which was commissioned by the provincial government to study the

situation in Montreal. It reported on March 28, 1991. La Presse of Montreal said the following:

"Poverty is spreading in the Montreal area. There are
615,000	people living in low-income households, half of them in Montreal proper".

There are other reports which show that, despite the fact that in Montreal many people gained economically during the period of 1985 to 1990, many people were big losers. That was principally the conclusion of the Cen-traide report, which I referred to already, under Paul Lacoste.
It said that Quebec went from having the fourth highest level of low-income households for families and individuals in 1979 to the highest rate in Canada for individuals, and the second highest after Newfoundland for families.
I spoke about food banks and the great proliferation of food banks in the Montreal area. Again, there is a report in this morning's paper with respect to the Sun Youth food bank in Montreal centre.
It said in the headline of The Gazette this morning: "Two Women Collapse, Two Men Fight in Food Lineup."
The Old Brewery Mission is another agency which provides food and shelter to homeless men.
It is known well by the Prime Minister.

It is known well, as my colleague says, by the Prime Minister. Reverend McCarthy, who is an outstanding individual, has been helping these men for years.
After 28 years of running the Old Brewery Mission, Reverend McCarthy is "disturbed by the dramatic increase in numbers of men showing up, and especially in the number under 25 who used to be comparatively rare among the mission's clientele and now account for around 60 per cent."
With respect to welfare, it says that the Government of Quebec is anticipating that costs for welfare will rise this year by $200 million.
A report from Quebec City by the minister Andre Bourbeau says: "The recession has caused at least 15,000 households to join Quebec's welfare roles since early fall. The total number of Quebec households on welfare now stands at 355,000."

That is the situation. It does not make me happy to recount those figures to the House of Commons. I was born in Montreal. I love Montreal. It is my city. It was once the metropolis of Canada. It was the economic engine for the entire province of Quebec, and I think we must look at that situation seriously to try to determine the causes.
What are the causes of this deplorable situation? If we look at the Picard report, the Secor report and some of the other reports, they say part of it is historical and part of it is recent.
Historically, according to some of these experts, Montreal had too many old-line industrial plants with skills geared to the old technology. Of course, as the old technology became outdated, for one reason or another Montreal did not adapt quickly enough and did not receive support to adapt quickly enough. I am not only speaking of the machinery and technology, but also the manpower, the trained workers.
Recently, however, I think we have to say to the government that some of its policies have also impacted on the situation and made it considerably worse. The free trade agreement has no doubt encouraged several businesses to go to the United States. On the radio this morning I heard a report-it was not with respect to Montreal but with respect to Toronto-about an agency which stated that it worked with 86 industrial firms which have moved from Toronto to the Buffalo area. We have not heard a similar report with respect to Montreal, but we know that certain companies, consolidating under the free trade agreement, moved their subsidiaries to the United States. One example is the Gillette plant, which was a subsidiary of the American company. It closed the plant in Montreal and consolidated its operations in Boston.
The free trade agreement has had an impact on this situation, which has to be looked at seriously. So has the goods and services tax. Everyone said, even those who agreed with the goods and services tax, expert after expert said that it was the wrong time to bring in the goods and services tax. It increased prices at a time when people were being laid off, when jobs were going scarce and people had a hard time coping with their economic situation.
I would submit that the free trade agreement, combined with the goods and services tax, has certainly contributed to the massive increase in cross-border shopping because it has increased the difference in prices between retail goods in Canada and retail goods in the United States.
Not only the GST, but other taxes have contributed to this recession and made the situation even worse in

Montreal. There was the report yesterday by the Ottawa-based firm, Global Economics, which pointed out that since 1984 all taxes have increased by $1,530 a year for middle-class taxpayers with a family of two.
Other things which might have been the cause and which require examination are the government's policies of deregulation and privatization, or one might say the dismantling of the infrastructure of Canada. Just a week or so ago we had the protest on Parliament Hill by the truckers. From time to time we have had other similar industries which have submitted that they have been extremely hurt by the policies of deregulation by the government. As for privatization, companies such as Air Canada and Petro-Canada also suffered from an employment point of view after privatization took place.
Put together all these policies, the policy for free trade with the United States, deregulation and privatization, and we see that we have had a dismantling of the Canadian economic infrastructure. I would submit that once we dismantle the Canadian economy and take away those things which made it a Canadian economy, sooner or later the political structure will disappear as well.
I could also refer to the high interest rates, which not only affect businesses in Montreal and employment in Montreal, but affect the situation right across the country.
One of the most important causes of this situation is the philosophy or policy of this government. If we look at the budgets of the government since 1984, we will see that it has adopted a series of policies which are more or less a doctrinaire commitment to a free market economy, a philosophy which says: "Let things be as they are, let the market operate as it will and everything will take care of itself". Government members continually rise in their places and condemn suggestions to spend money to stimulate the economy.
They describe that as throwing money at the problem. I think that where a country spends its money shows where its priorities are. There is no doubt that money has to be spent on certain items if we are going to reinvigorate the Montreal economy.
Mr. Speaker, you are indicating to me that I only have a minute left. I have enough material here to go on for a quite considerable length of time.
I am sure that in its response the government will refer to certain things it has done. It will refer to a contract to Canadair. It will refer to some things it did for the
pharmaceutical industry. It will refer to the new agency that will be set up under the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It will refer to the program for older workers adjustment.
These things, while good in themselves, are isolated ad hoc policies which have not dealt with the problem that needs to be dealt with. If they had been successful, we would not have the situation I have described. These policies are not enough. Montreal needs much, much more.
I have a report here which says that the POWA program is a cruel lottery for the "laid off". It is underfunded, it does not have enough money.
My final remarks are that we need political will, political commitment to create jobs in the Montreal area. It can be done. It has been done in other countries. Liberals did it in the past. Between 1965 and 1980, there was a 5.6 per cent unemployment rate in Canada. That is because we believed in a mixed economy.
I encourage the government to look at the situation in Montreal once again and come forward with some positive policies. If it does so during the debate today, I will withdraw my motion and give it credit for doing so.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to what my colleague had to say, especially about some programs the Conservative government implemented to protect workers living in the province of Quebec, and particularly in Montreal. I would like my colleague to give us more details about two programs that have had a negative impact on POWA a program for workers affected by changes in the industries and plant closings due to economic upheavals, or as some would say, due to the free trade deal. There is also the other program the hon. member has mentioned. I would like more information on that one, because as an member, I have received a lot of complaints from people who wanted to benefit from POWA and other programs put in place by the federal government to help workers when they lose their jobs. I do not think these programs are working at all. Like my colleague has just said, they have become more like a lottery for the laid off.

Mr. Speaker, for POWA, I do not have figures for the province of Quebec, but I do have overall statistics for Canada showing that the amount of money available is inadequate. For example, I have here an article published in the Winnipeg Free Press, on May 23, 1991, where it says:

Only $73 million of the promised $150 million was used in those first two years for the program for older worker adjustment, providing benefits to 2,244 ex-workers. That is for the entire country, 2,244 ex-workers. I already put on the record, and these were not my statistics, that in the Montreal region there are 188,000 workers who have been laid off in the last two years and are now out of work.
The article goes on to say that, despite the steady stream of plant closings and business bankruptcies, only a tiny fraction have been declared by POWA's joint federal-provincial labour department committee to meet the major layoff test, and therefore qualify for designation under the program.
In Ontario, only 39 qualified. I do not have the figures for Quebec. In answer to the hon. member, while the government has some programs which in theory look good on paper, they are drastically underfunded and do not meet the seriousness of the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Montreal for bringing to the attention of the rest of the country the problems of Montreal.
I would like to refer him to the Question Period last week when different members were pursuing the question of the economic health of Montreal. The minister stood up and said that they were trying to develop a plan because of Montreal's poor health. When another member got up and asked him about the future of Winnipeg, the Minister of Finance stood up and said: "You do not need a plan because you have good macro policies".
I wanted to bring this to the attention of the member and ask a question. I think in previous governments, particularly in the Liberal government in the 1970s and 1980s, there was a good mix between federal activity and provincial and municipal activity in support of regional base plans. There was the Montreal base region, the Winnipeg base region and other parts of the country. In the absence of having coherent plans for these cities, you end up with the extreme opposite. You end up with people competing against each other and running the

risk of having plans which are contrary to the interests of the country.
For example, there is the story both in Winnipeg and Montreal of the competition over the CF-18 plane. That was a debate which should not have taken place in this country, pitting one region against the other.
I would ask the member if he could perhaps elaborate on the need for city base plans, not only in Montreal but across the country. The federal government should show leadership financially, morally and with the expertise in the Public Service so that people appreciate the government's understanding of their needs in terms of unemployment, poverty, training and getting the proper businesses set up. This is a holistic approach which deserves the interest of the federal government. In fact, one of the big surprises that we have is the total absence of planning on the part of this government.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is correct. Liberal governments over the years believed in a mixed economy. We believed in the market system but we believed that in a country such as Canada where we have 25 million people dispersed over a large area, right up against the giant economy of the United States, it was necessary for us to have certain government support programs and certain government economic intervention. Over the years that approach worked. We had the greatest eras of prosperity in this country under Liberal governments in the fifties, sixties and seventies.
I pointed out that from 1965 to 1980 the average rate of employment was 5.6 per cent. The government always refers to the two years of 1981-82. We had a recession but it was no worse than the recession which is going on right now.
We believed in doing things to deal with recessions. We did not have this doctrinaire belief, this 19th century belief that the marketplace would take care of itself and all situations and that there would be a trickling down effect which would help small businesses and the economy generally.
In response to the member's question with respect to municipalities and planning, the Canadian Federation of Municipalities has for years recommended a joint federal, provincial and municipal program to reconstruct municipal infrastructure; roads, bridges, sewers, water systems, anti-pollution systems, ports, airports, transpor-

lation systems and power systems. The government has continually rejected the recommendations of the Canadian Federation of Municipalities.
Not only would that program provide employment, it would also provide the necessary infrastructure for business to invest in those municipalities and invest in an environment which would be more conducive to profit making, creation of jobs and economic growth.
This government has its philosophy. I must say that previous Conservative governments did not have that same philosophy. The government of Mr. Diefenbaker did not have this doctrinaire belief in the free market economy. It also believed in a mixed economy. The government of Mr. Clark did not have this doctrinaire approach.
It seems with the coming to power of the Conservatives in 1984 under the present Prime Minister they were wed to the policies of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan, which are a disaster for this country and are not really in the tradition of political parties of all stripes in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I was wondering if the member could explain how he rationalizes the attitude of the province of Quebec. It is clear that the province is responsible for cities and municipalities within the province. How can he rationalize that view with his present view, apparently, of the Constitution that the Government of Canada should directly interfere with municipal financing and municipal activity?
Is it the policy of the Liberal Party that we should go right over the head of the province of Quebec and deal directly with the municipality so that the municipality would not have to worry about Quebec City? Should the federal government handle roads and subsidies for roads and direct where traffic ought to go?
Is it his view and that of his party that because there is unemployment in Montreal-there is in other cities in other parts of the country-and because of the incompetence of the Quebec government we ought to go at that problem and deal with that problem? Is that the view of the Liberal Party?

Mr. Speaker, not at all. That is not our view. When we were in power we had a department of housing and urban renewal which worked closely with the provinces and the municipalities but always recognized the principal jurisdiction of the provinces.
Right now there are several departments in the federal government: the Department of Transport which deals with railways, airports, ports, canals; the Department of the Environment; and the new agency being set up under the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The only complaint I have about that is that they did not consult close enough with Quebec. I am not suggesting that the federal government run roughshod over provincial jurisdiction. I am suggesting that they sit down with the province of Quebec in this case and the city of Montreal and develop a plan whereby those things which are under federal jurisdiction, such as transportation and certain types of housing, can be done in conjunction with the city. They have been done that way in the past in a very positive, effective way, and they can be done that way again.

Mr. Speaker, Montrealers who were watching the first speaker this morning, the mover of the motion before the House today, must have noticed how good the opposition is at blaming the government and how little they have to offer in the way of solutions. Not a word, and I would be embarrassed if I were them, Mr. Speaker, not a word about their failure to deal with the situation in Montreal during the many years they were in power here in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk about Montreal and the economy of this major Canadian city, a number of factors should be put into perspective. Today, unfortunately, Montreal is faced with a number of economic problems. With 207,000 unemployed in April 1991, the Montreal metropolitan area has an unemployment rate of 13.1 per cent, which is unacceptable.
However, this situation did not arise in a matter of months or a few years, I think it is correct to say that Montreal's economy started to falter in the middle of the 1960s, and for the next ten years, it steadily declined.
June 4, 1991

As far as job creation is concerned, Montreal's performance has been lacklustre for the past 30 years. It ranks below Halifax, Mr. Speaker. It created one-third of the jobs created by Calgary. Toronto had about the same number of jobs in 1961. Today, Toronto has half a million more jobs than Montreal. The situation worsened at the beginning of the 80s. During the past ten years, Mr. Speaker, Montreal has ranked twenty-first among Canada's 25 metropolitan regions, on job creation.
What is the underlying cause of the economic malaise that has affected Montreal's economy for so many years? The cause is structural because, as was said earlier by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, historically, Montreal has specialized in producing consumer goods- mostly for the Canadian market-including food, beverages, tobacco, textiles, clothing, leather items and furniture. As international competition strengthened in these sectors, many jobs in Montreal were lost.
When our government was elected in 1984, it immediately addressed the task of turning the situation around. The point I want to make today, Mr. Speaker, is that our government is the first one since many years that did not remain indifferent to Montreal's problems. In fact, a lot has been done since this government came to power. However, we did not go in without a plan. No, Mr. Speaker, we wanted that every initiative bore fruit. So our interventions followed an approach favouring the development of Montreal based on its many strengths in areas such as high technology, for example, tourism and cultural activities, design, finance, commerce and international activities.
For we should not forget that Montreal does not only have problems. It has, for example, a modern manufacturing sector which, as a whole, made considerable progress during the last decades, whether it be in plastics, electronic products or transport equipment.
Montreal has many assets, and that is why we decided to rely on these strengths to revitalize its economy. That does not mean we should not do something for some less advantaged areas on its territory. In this regard, let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that in February 1988, this government set up a $35 million special program for the economic recovery of eastern Montreal. In May 1990, it

was the turn of south western Montreal businesses to avail themselves of a similar program with a $15 million envelope.
To complement its action, the Department of Industry, Science and Technology announced that it would make available a $6.5 million funding for the implementation of special projects by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Later on today, we will be able to provide you with more details on those various initiatives that we can rightly be proud of.
As I mentioned a few moments ago, this government has been very active in Montreal since 1984. Our action took place in sectors considered a priority for the development of Montreal.
In the area of research and development, I want to remind honourable members that our government tried to pass as fast as it could Bill C-22 amending the Patents Act. This bill gave back to Montreal the level of research and development activity it lacked for so long and it encouraged several important drug companies to implement research and development programs totalling tens of millions of dollars.
Mr. Speaker, this government has invested more than 2.5 billion dollars in new money to support initiatives in science and technology. Through the Networks of Centres of Excellence Program, the Canadian government has been able to give real support to at least two Montreal networks. For example, the Institute for Robotics and Intelligent Systems will bring together the best Canadian scientists in research on expert systems and intelligent robots.
Through the same program, this government granted a 12.3 million dollars contribution for the respiratory diseases network which is based in Montreal, in order to find better treatment and better means of prevention. The work of both networks dovetails with that of other institutions and will contribute to the reputation and economic renewal of Montreal.
If there is another area where our government did not spare his efforts for Montreal, it is that of high technology. For example, it supported the creation of the Techno-parc Montreal Metropolitan, which will facilitate the emergence of new businesses, the intensification, transfer and diffusion of high technology.

Mr. Speaker, our government has also not forgotten the aeronautical and aerospace industries. The aeronautical industry in Montreal creates jobs for more than
40.000	people, which makes it, by far, the single most important high technology sector in the area. Bombardier-Canadair, with which our government has cooperated on several occasions in recent years, particularly with a contribution of $43 million for the development of its regional transport jet, the famous stretched aircraft, should expand noticeably in the next few years.
The future of CAE Electronics, the world's number one builder of flight simulators for commercial aircraft, looks also very good, since the demand for this product should continue to grow in the years to come.
Mr. Speaker, as regards the aerospace industry, allow me to mention again that our government has established the Canadian Space Agency in the Montreal region. This initiative will have a positive effect in promoting space related activities in Quebec. Already, a great number of firms, under the umbrella of Spar Aerospace Limited, with whom our government signed, in 1986, a memorandum of understanding for $300 million, take an active part in the development of this important industry.
In Quebec, some 60 companies employing close to
7.000	workers build equipment or components used for transmitting and receiving voice, image and data communications. It is expected that the international market for telecommunication material will increase at an annual rate of 8 per cent between now and the year 2000. Mr. Speaker, when one considers that the companies of the telecommunication sector are almost all located in the Montreal area, it is easy to understand that their possibilities for growth are particularly good.
Mr. Speaker, our government recognizes the important role that the tourism and cultural industries can play in the development of Montreal. For that reason, those industries have benefited from important federal contributions in recent years.
Major facilities have been built and have helped Montreal become a world-class destination for tourists. Soon, the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts will have more
than doubled its capacity for exhibits. The Montreal Botanical Garden, with its Japanese garden and its insectarium, has become one of Montreal's most important tourist attractions.
The old port area, where the Canadian government will have invested a total of $65 million by the end of 1992, will also become a major tourist attraction in North America.
The Lachine Canal, that will be opened to boaters after restoration work is completed, will be reconstructed according to the original course. The priming of the locks is scheduled for October 1991. In the east, Mr. Speaker, important developments are planned, including a basin, the Bonsecours basin, and a large multi-purpose area on the Jacques-Cartier pier. That area will be used to accommodate large crowds and to hold special events.
The Department of Industry, Science and Technology has also spent more than $2 million on various feasibility studies for the establishment of the Museum of Science and Technology.
Again near the St. Lawrence, the government is committed to spending more than $10 million to create a centre for archaeology and history at Pointe-a-Calliere, to illustrate Montreal's evolution as a commercial city.
Just across the old port area, Mr. Speaker, our government has recently confirmed its commitment to invest nearly $40 million on ile Sainte-Helene for the development of the "pare des ties", which will become the biggest park in Montreal. In the biosphere will be the water and environment interpretation centre, and development costs will be paid by our government.
The "pare des lies" will be inaugurated in 1992, the year in which Montreal will celebrate the 350th anniversary of its foundation. Moreover, in order to show how important that anniversary is to our government, we are committed to spending $10 million for the organization of major activities related to the 1992 celebrations.
In addition to museum equipments, large amounts of money have been invested, Mr. Speaker, in the renovation of theatres and music halls in Montreal, and financial assistance to major cultural events has helped maintain their attractiveness for Montreal's tourists.

Our government, Mr. Speaker, has strived to reaffirm Montreal's vocation as an international city. Even if one of my colleagues will speak on that aspect of our mandate later on today, I would like to take this opportunity to remind you that the federal government supported the Societe du centre de conferences interna-tionalcs de Montreal in order to conduct a feasibility study to create an international centre in Montreal and to promote concrete initiatives for the development of international activities in this city.
It is also with a $10 million grant that a United Nations organisation, the Multilateral Fund for the Montreal Protocol on the Ozone Layer, chose our city as the site of its permanent office.
Mr. Speaker, all these initiatives of our government show very well the development potential of Montreal. Moreover, different projects which are under way all over the city are an indication that the situation is changing in Montreal. These projects are also an eloquent proof of the interest that the government of Canada has taken in Montreal since 1984, and of the support it intends to bring in the coming years.

Mr. Speaker, the minister mentioned that the government has introduced several programs for the Montreal region, but the situation has not improved. In Montreal, the economy is still in shambles. The minister said, for example, that the government has introduced a program for East Montreal. But what is the result? How many jobs were created with this program?
If this program was good for East Montreal why is it that we still find in this area an unemployment rate of 20 per cent and that 25 per cent of the population is on welfare? How can we explain this situation if the programs are so good and efficient?
The minister mentioned Canadair. We are very happy for Canadair and in this case, it is a success, but it is not enough for the Montreal region. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, why this government has chosen to ignore the Picard Report, a commission it created.

The things mentioned by the minister in his speech are truly an ad hoc band-aid approach. They remind me of

the doctor, after his patient is dead, telling the family that he had given aspirin, Alka-Seltzer and such minor medications to the patient before he died.
This patient, the city of Montreal, requires something more than aspirin and band-aids. I ask the minister: When will the government finally announce a substantial, comprehensive response to the Picard commission, a commission that made 84 recommendations?
The government set up the commission and yet we have not had any response to the 84 recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace shoots from the hip-that is how he began his speech this morning-by quoting newspaper articles when we would have expected him, as the mover of today's motion, to give us examples of what his party would have done in previous years and what positive measures it would propose now to help Montreal.
It seems that he did not read the Picard Report, Mr. Speaker, that he is not giving any consideration to what we are achieving right now because the great majority of the programs I mentioned in my speech are directly derived from individual recommendations contained in the Picard Report.
In fact, that report recommended government intervention in areas of its jurisdiction and never proposed that the federal government should take responsibility for the economic recoveiy of the entire island of Montreal because it would have been totally ridiculous to propose such a thing. Essentially it would have been like saying that the federal government should submit itself to all provincial and municipal governments in Canada and carry out the responsibilities of all levels of government.
Because we are always in contact with the municipal authorities of Montreal and the suburbs and with the provincial government, I know that nobody wants the federal government to forcibly impose its way of doing things. The elected people at all levels expect the federal government to be a facilitator in the implementation of the programs and projects they propose. That is what we have been doing since 1984, Mr. Speaker, in the most complete harmony with the other levels of government.

June 4, 1991
Supply

Mr. Speaker, I was involved in the House when we had a massive debate, to a large extent led by the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, on Bill C-22 involving the removal of patent protection. The minister alluded to the increase in employment as a result of that measure which was opposed by the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace.
I was also in the House when the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace led the opposition against the sale of Canadair to Bombardier. That sale enabled Bombardier to become a leading manufacturer of aircraft. I was wondering if the minister could outline the exact numbers of additional people who are now working in Montreal in the high-tech aircraft industry as a result of that measure. In other words, outline the measures that this government has used, opposed by the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, that have enabled more employment in Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, the example just cited by my hon. colleague about Bombardier and Canadair is a perfect example of the proper application of privatization by this government.
Canadair was going nowhere when Bombardier took over its operations from the Government of Canada. Because of the knowledge and competence of the private sector which took over this company, it is now a viable business. At the time of the takeover, Canadair was reducing the number of its employees. On the day of the takeover, the employment at Canadair was less than
5.000	people. At the present time there are 7,500 people employed at Canadair. On the day of the launching of the new regional jet, the president of Canadair told me that within the next few months they expect to have over
10.000	people working at Canadair.
These are high-paying, high-tech jobs and are the type of jobs that this government wants to generate to really reinforce the economy of Montreal.
When this government took power in 1984, we decided that never again would we repeat the errors of the previous government who spent and indebted this country for generations to come by creating make-shift jobs
that were very good for electoral purposes, but did absolutely nothing for the economy of Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport complained that the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace was quoting from newspapers. I would like to quote to him from the throne speech where in the conclusion the Prime Minister says:
My government will work with Canadians to achieve its goals of unity, prosperity and responsive government so that all Canadians feel themselves a part of this country, so that all Canadians have an equal opportunity to share in its bounty, so that all can see themselves reflected in its constitution and so that all will find the fulfilment of their aspirations in its future.
I want to ask the minister, do the words in the throne speech "equal opportunity to share in its bounty" mean sharing this bounty by lining up at food banks where the lines are getting longer and longer? Does sharing this bounty mean that the Montreal school boards have to give free breakfasts to children before they can teach them? Is this what the throne speech means by sharing the bounty, the wealth, the prosperity of this country?
Very specifically, Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the minister what concrete plans does his government have to reduce and finally eliminate the food banks in Montreal, Toronto, Windsor, and almost every major city in this country? What concrete plans does this government have so that the boards of education will not have to subsidize breakfasts and free milk to children before they can be taught in schools.
I asked the minister and this government following the last throne speech and I got no answer. I am giving this minister an opportunity on behalf of his government to give us some concrete plans and programs for eliminating food banks and subsidizing children's food.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the members on the opposite side think that Montrealers have forgotten what their government has imposed on them over the years when they were in power.
They are the party that fought the adoption of Bill C-22 which was such a sweeping tool for the pharmaceutical industry to create more jobs. It is that government that fought the working and the action of la Caisse de depots in Montreal that was such a wonderful tool for helping the local industries.
It was that party that fought for two years, with the help of their Liberal friends in the Senate, to prevent the
June 4. 1991

adoption of Bill C-21 which is now providing the necessary tools for people to move from low technology, low paying jobs, through training necessary to apply for the better paying jobs in high technology fields. They are the ones that are at fault for doing these things that have been such a detriment to the economy of the Montreal area.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say, in the spirit of this lack of partisanship, I think we have started off on a very bad foot this morning. It seems to me that this debate is going absolutely nowhere.
We have members on the government side saying it is not their fault that Montreal has a 25 per cent welfare roll, UIC roll; it is not their fault that unemployment is about 14 per cent in the city of Montreal.
On the other side we have our Liberal colleagues saying it is not their fault either, the deterioration of the city of Montreal has occurred under the present government.
I suppose for people who are listening and watching us on television it is hard to understand exactly where this debate is going. I think we should go back to the sense of the motion of my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace and look at it as an opportunity for the government not to wash its hands of this affair and say look, it is your fault, you Liberals, because of C-22. It is your fault because of your so-called opposition to the elargissement ties pouvoirs de la Caisse de depot du Quebec.
We have right now, this morning, an excellent opportunity for the government side to say that they have made a few mistakes and there are some things they can do. "Yes, Mr. Deputy from Notre-Dame-de-Grace, you have some good points, but we do not accept all of them. We are all somewhat responsible for the mess we find ourselves in". That is what I would like to have heard listening for the past hour or so, but I have not heard it.
I am a Montrealer and I would like to give you first of all, some of what I have seen as a Montrealer. I live in downtown Montreal, and I also represent a number of cities on the south shore of Montreal, all of them having been affected by this downturn in the economy, this recession. First let me give you some statistics on the Montreal area.
Supply
First of all, 25 per cent of Montrealers receive unemployment insurance or welfare benefits. Let me talk about these people, because we have a strong tendency here in the House to quote figures, but 25 per cent of the people depend on unemployment insurance or welfare. That means that 175 persons per day must apply for unemployment insurance or welfare benefits, 175 persons per day.
As you know, much has been said about Argentina's foreign policy and disparecidos, those people who disappear. One day they are present, but the next, they are gone.
Well, that also happens in Canada, that happens in Montreal. We call them economic disparecidos, those who disappear from the economic picture. These people disappear when they lose their jobs. Losing your job sometimes means losing your house, your family, and finally, you end up losing hope. We have nearly reached that point, Mr. Speaker. People have practically no hope anymore. I do not mean-and I hope that the government will understand-that the government has done nothing. In fact, the government has tried to correct the situation, but the question asked by my hon. friend for Notre-Dame-de-Grace is excellent, because he recognized that the government has made some efforts, but he wanted to know the results. Where is the beef? Where is the result? What are the results of your efforts in Montreal?
I think one must understand that Montrealers blame the federal government, among others, for not delivering results. It is obvious. The government cannot claim that it did everything it could.
Much was said about Laurent Picard's report. I read it and I found it excellent. It contained many recommendations, not 84, but 86, and those were good ones. But in an analysis of this government's behaviour, the editorial writer of The Gazette was saying in late February 1991: "The federal government ignored almost all of these 86 recommendations." This is not a New Democratic member or a Liberal member, but a non partisan editorial writer who said that the Picard report, sponsored by the government, was almost totally ignored by this government.

June 4, 1991
Supply
Mr. Speaker, there are things we can do and I want to take this opportunity today not to criticize this government-some have done it and others will-but to suggest some alternatives, to make some suggestions that the government can use and that are not new. I do not think these are new to the government, because it already heard several of the suggestions that I will make. But I think it is nevertheless an excellent opportunity to remind this government which actions it should take to specifically deal with this unemployment problem, with the deterioration of the social and local infrastructure in Montreal.
I saw very recently the request of the CSN in Montreal, and they gave me a number of actions that they thought were necessary to boost the economy in Montreal.
In going over their suggestions, I find they are quite sensible. Let me tell you what the CSN in Montreal is suggesting. In order to boost the economy in Montreal, we must deal with the issue of the interest rates, which are still too high. I know that the rates are down, and it is a good sign, but the problem with the interest rates in Canada is that they had remained high for so long because of this government's policies that now that they are down a little, companies which could normally invest money and help revive the economy are almost running out of it. We do not have what we call a big pool of risk capital, it is dry. The government needs to continue to intervene to lower interest rates, although up to now it did not do much to lower them. They have gone down despite government programs. A lowering of interest rates is vital, there is no doubt about it, because there won't be any economic recovery without it.
Now, I would like to talk about the POW. It was referred to briefly a short while ago, but I should say it is extremely important for Quebec and Montreal. Have you ever heard about the POW? This is a program which was established shortly before the signing of the free trade agreement. The government had said: "We know that people working in the clothing industry, for example, will be adversely affected by the FTA and that is why we will be setting up a program to help and retrain these people so they can find another job. Mr. Speaker, if there is an area about which I receive a lot of complaints, it is certainly the POW. This program is not working well. To be eligible, people must have worked a certain
number of years in a soft sector of the industry. But what is a soft sector in Montreal? Most industries in that city are in a soft sector. So, how do we define a soft sector? People who believed the government when it was saying that the POW would protect workers affected by the free trade accord are in deep trouble.
I could mention a number of people I met who were working in the women's clothing industry. I remember very well Mrs. Lorraine Vaillancourt, a member of the FTQ. She is really concern about these workers, because they have very little protection, and that is why the POW needs to be improved. I hope the minister, when he comes back, will explain to us what he intends to do about this program.
When we talk about economic recovery in Montreal, we must also talk about taxes. Taxes are killing the middle class. Tkxes are killing industries. And what about the GST? Frankly, that tax which was supposed to be visible, to be revenue neutral, is none of that. We know that it is a milking cow which is going to produce not the $18 billion forecasted, but up to $30 billion per year for the government, if my information is correct. That money comes from the taxpayer's pocket and that is the reason why people are going shopping elsewhere. Quebecers, and especially Montrealers, have to do their shopping outside Canada, in Plattsburg and Burlington, precisely to escape the clutches of this federal government which has taxed almost every product and service. Quebecers are trying to avoid this tax. They have become nomads, shoppers who have to seek out good deals wherever they are, even if it means shopping outside Canada.
Consequently, I think that GST must be abolished. It must go. It is an unfair tax, a tax which creates a lot more problems than it has solved and a tax which, even now, forces Quebecers to turn their backs on their own country. The real tragedy in this is that we are forced to turn our backs on our own workers in Montreal, on the lady who makes clothing in a Montreal plant because we can get them cheaper in States.
It is a fact. I think that this government can take some steps towards solving these problems, but I must add that as long as the GST remains, these problems will persist.
June 4, 1991

Another issue was raised by CNTU, that is tax reform in general. My colleague from Mississauga South, whose speech was excellent, wanted to know how we could settle Quebec's problems if we cannot deal directly with the municipalities, or if we must always work with the provincial level.
When we're talking about tax reform, nothing is more normal than to cooperate with the provinces. I am not aware of any circumstances when Quebec has refused to accept initiatives undertaken by the federal government. The question is about cooperation, not about forcing a measure nor presenting an ultimatum. It is all about cooperation. And herein lies one of this government's problems. We have seen an example of it when the minister wanted to create a department of regional development for Quebec. I think it's the fortieth federal department encroaching on Quebec's jurisdiction.
This is not what we would like to see the federal government do. We want the federal government to work with us, we don't want it to tell us what to do. I think there is enough room for manoeuvre. Quebec is always intelligent enough, I think, to accept a federal presence as long as the provincial jurisdiction is respected.
So, we are talking about tax reform. I was here, yesterday, when the leader of the official opposition and the leader of our party, the New Democratic Party, asked questions about tax reform and how Quebecers were taxed. The Prime Minister was laughing throughout those questions. He thought it was hilarious, and he was laughing in our faces. It's true. That is the picture that we get on the screen. Consumers can now see what the government is doing and how arrogant it is. I have seen such arrogant behavior on both sides of the House. I also remember how arrogant the previous government was.
But now the middle class is an endangered species because it is taxed too heavily. The minister recognized it yesterday, the one who is staring at me in amazement. He said people are taxed, overtaxed even, and he is right. Somebody has to pay taxes. But he was quoted in the press. Maybe he now wants to withdraw his words but he did say that someone had to pay taxes. He then admitted that the middle class was paying more and that as a member of that class he was also paying more and that it was necessary. I say that is not necessary for there are other ways of collecting taxes. Corporations can be
Supply
taxed. I know that the U.S. have a minimum tax on corporations. I think it is 20 per cent. I believe business is working as well in the U.S. as it is in Canada, if not better. When we talk of boosting Montreal's economy, we cannot refuse to consider a major tax reform to create an environment that would allow such a recovery.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you why the CNTU has formulated a number of suggestions. I can also tell you that in my region, the UPA, Union des producteurs agricoles, has endorsed suggestions quite similar to that of the CNTU. This union and this group of farmers made these suggestions because they believe that there is still time for the govemement to act. They believe they have solutions to propose. They believe that, with a minimum of good will, we can find solutions together, we can improve Montreal's economy as well as that of Quebec and of Canada as a whole.
So, even if we admit that the government has done a couple of things to offset the problems of Montreal and elsewhere, I repeat that what we saw is clearly too little and, unfortunately, too late. It is not what this government had promised us before signing the free trade agreement and certainly not what it had promised before being re-elected in 1988.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member was putting words in my mouth I felt I should stand up and correct the impression that he left with the public. He was referring to a report that came out by Patrick Grady of a company here in Ottawa called Global Economics Ltd. which very correctly pointed out that the income tax level in Canada is higher than in other countries of the world. In the same report he also pointed out that we pay less than half the taxes for our social policy fields. We pay less sales tax than other countries and our corporate taxes are comparable to other countries.
Today we are talking about the economy in Montreal but the hon. member failed to mention this. Mr. Grady praises reform of the corporate taxation system saying, "changes have boosted investment in economic growth and in job creation". He also generally approves of the 7 per cent goods and services tax introduced in January: "The corporate tax changes are improving the economic efficiency by reducing the degree of tax induced distor-

June 4, 1991
Supply
tion in investment, decision-making across industries, and acid types," he says in the report. "This leads to a pattern of investment and economic activity that is more productive and conducive to economic growth and employment criticism". Grady said: "The Tories have eliminated some tax incentives that had prompted companies to make the wrong investment decisions as well an over-all lowering of corporate tax rates has kept Canadian companies from moving operations to the United States".
The report that is quoted widely by both the opposition parties is not complete in its quotation by the opposition parties. I want to ask the hon. member whose party, the New Democratic Party, the socialist party of Canada, wants to increase taxes on corporations which in doing so would place them in an uncompetitive position with their neighbours, our competitors, not only to the south but internationally. If the hon. member looks at this report, and studies it carefully, he will see that our corporate tax rate is right in line with most other countries of the world. I think the only other country that taxes a much wider spread is Japan. I think Japan is the only one, and Japan has a lower income tax rate as well, but far greater productivity than we have here. It all has to be weighed.
When the hon. member is making his selective reports, why does he not come out and give the government credit where the report gave the government credit, that in fact tax reform has done a good job in making the tax system fairer for corporations? We are realizing $1 billion more in income from corporations. We have cut out a lot of the cute little deals that the Liberals put in the tax act, that you could write off. We have taken those out of there to make the tax system much fairer. Why does the hon. member not stand up and congratulate the government for those moves?

Mr. Speaker, I started off this debate saying that there were things that this government has done. I would not stand here today and say that it was all white or all black. There have been some things, but I will be darned if I will be accused here in this House of saying that I have not given the government credit for some things. I have said that the government has done some things, but not enough.
When the minister talks to me about how the government has reined in the corporations as far as tax liability
is concerned. I do not believe him. Canadians do not believe him. It is not fair for him to stand up here day in and day out to continually say: "These people are wrong and they are only right when they agree with us". That is wrong.
The point I am trying to make in this report is this: "PM laughs off attack on taxes". I was here and I saw it.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to just mention to you, in the same report that we are talking about, we are talking about corporate taxes.
That is nonsense.
You raised the subject, as far as corporate taxes are concerned. Let me speak to the Chair because I am just learning and I do not want to be direct to the minister.
You've been here three years. What do you mean you're learning?

Mr. Speaker, this man says I have been here three years. I thank him for his compliment. I have been here exactly a year and three months.
But, Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to your attention that he brought up corporate taxes, I did not. I would like to refer to the same article. It says, and it is not difficult to understand.
Are you quoting from the Sun?

I am quoting from the Ottawa Sun, Robert Fife, Parliamentary Bureau. As for corporate taxes, the tax load of corporate taxes, the tax load declined to 2.6 per cent of GDP in 1989, compared with 3.4 in 1984.
But we took a lot of the write-offs out.

Mr. Speaker, whenever you bring up a point-and here you go- that the government does not agree with, it says: "Yes, but", or it will shoot the messenger, or it will say that was the other government, or it will say that minister is no longer here.
This is absolutely unreal. Canadians demand more of us than this. Mr. Speaker, let me ask you if I can do this. I have had my say. I am going to sit down. There is a little bit of time left. I am going to ask this of the people on the other side. We have talked about whose responsibility it is. We all realize that Montreal is in trouble. We all realize that there are some things to do. I am going to sit
June 4. 1991

down right now. The government can have the rest of my time and it can tell me what it is going to do.

I certainly cannot pass up an opportunity like that because we have done a tremendous amount of work, not only for Montreal but for everyone across this country.
Tax reform and the free trade agreement, which the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party have opposed all along, are going to bring benefits to this country for years and years to come. There is no question about it.
As a matter of fact, we have seen examples already where our exports are up in many areas of the economy. This helps the entire area. Montreal has had a tremendously difficult time, and nobody talks about it. Nobody stands up and talks about it.
I think the political atmosphere has had something to do with people making investment decisions in this country. If there is anything we can do in this country, it is to bring our country together in a unified, caring way for one another across this country. I think that will reap benefits for Montreal and the province of Quebec and all regions of this country.
For far too long we have tended in this country to point fingers instead of hold hands. We have been more apt to say goodbye instead of say hello to one another. I think one of the problems that the province of Quebec is experiencing is this political uncertainty.
It is our fault.

No, it is not. It is all our faults. It is the fault of all Canadians. It is the problem of all Canadians. I do not think we know one another well enough. I think that is probably one of the biggest problems we have in this country. We do not know one another well enough. We in Ontario do not know the westerners well enough; the westerners do not know the Quebecers well enough. It can go right across, from coast to coast. This is a huge country. It is 5,000 miles wide. We have a small population. We do not have the same opportunities that smaller countries have to get to know one another. That is our problem. We have to get to know one another in this country.
I am going to tell you that part of the problem in Montreal is just the political uncertainty. I do not think there is any question about that. I think people making
Supply
investment decisions and deciding to expand or establish businesses look at those things. I am sure they do. They look for political certainty.
There is a story this morning in The Financial Post of concern in Ontario now about investment decisions. A group has made a statement. I do not know if it is true or not, but its experience has been that people are taking a very close look at what the government in Ontario is doing now for investment decisions because of its political situation. So that comes into it. Nobody talks about that and I cannot understand why.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for LaSalle-Emard has the floor for 10 minutes.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to deal with an issue which is very dear to all of us, and certainly to us Liberals, namely Montreal's economical situation. I particularly want to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, supported by the hon. member for Saint-Denis, for attempting to force this recalcitrant government to recognize the slump my city of Montreal is in.
Our city, Mr. Speaker, is not about to regain its former status of Canadian metropolis, as Brian Mulroney had promised it would in 1984. A close look at its situation brings about this sudden realization. Let me mention a few data: in April 1991, unemployment stood at 13.6 per cent; no other major city in Canada shows such a pitiful record. There were 17.6 per cent unemployed among youths between the age of 20 and 24. Youths are our future. In southwestern Montreal which I represent with my colleague, the unemployment rate stands at 16.2 per cent; 17 per cent of young people drop out of high-school before graduating. The true unemployment figure is close to 30 per cent, 10 000 people, Mr. Speaker, have been victims of mass lay offs as in the case of Coleco, Simmons, Sidbec and VIA Rail. Come to my riding in the southwest of Montreal and you will see all the plants which have closed down. You will be in a position to understand the situation. For each plant which has

June 4, 1991
Supply
closed down, there are thousands of employees who have lost their jobs and this puts stress on their families.
Montreal slump, Mr. Speaker, is a national disgrace for which this government must accept a large part of responsibility. It is under his administration that Montreal's economic erosion started.
The causes are obvious: devastating economic policies on the part of the Conservatives; the high level of our dollar, which closed at 87 cents yesterday. That is ridiculous, absolutely absurd and it is killing us! High interest rates. How could we develop industries in Montreal when we are crushed by interest rates 3 percent higher than in the United States? There were no adjustments made after the Free Trade Agreement was signed. This government and this minister had promised adjustment measures to help our industries and our workers who are the big loosers in this deal. What did we get? Absolutely nothing. Training and retraining? What for? It is ineffective, unproductive and redundant. Research and development? Shame on this government for slashing funding to nothing!
Mr. Speaker, this government simply lacks vision for Montreal. It is incapable of delivering the goods. The federal government is running a one man show. There is no coordination, no consultation with the people involved, no agreement with Quebec, no agreement with the city of Montreal. You have just heard the announcement made by the Health Minister concerning the regional development of Quebec. No consultations with the people involved and no intention of harmonizing their involvement. The government has no agenda, no vision and no political will to act. Here is the Conservative track record for you!
Mr. Speaker, Montreal is the driving force of the Quebec economy. Left unattended, the whole province stands to suffer. Fortunately, the slump Montreal is in is not irreversible. It can get out of it. Solutions do exist. The key is an expression of political will on the part of the federal government to work in concert with the city and the province. Unfortunately, the Tories are showing no such will. Brian Mulroney and his government never
showed the will to do anything concrete and reasonable. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the Tories do not understand what Montreal needs. It is absolutely appalling that no Cabinet member from Quebec is taking part in this debate. They let a minister from Toronto defend Montreal. That goes to show how unreasonable the Tories are.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. First, it is traditional in this House that we do not talk about the presence or the absence of a minister. Second, the minister was in the House and delivered his speech. He had to leave on government business. He will be coming back. I think it is very unfair of the hon. member to take that kind of a shot at him. He asked to be excused and he will be back. I trust the hon. member will take that as advice.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate a minister from Toronto who spoke out for Montreal.

I am quite sure when it comes time to talk about Toronto, the ministers from Montreal will be in this House and will defend Toronto. I am also sure that when we look at what this government does, the Montreal ministers must defend Toronto a great, great deal.

Mr. Speaker, what is the Conservative philosophy? Retire as soon as possible. Act only for political reasons. Forget sustained intervention. Forget consultation, in other words, laissez-faire.
Mr. Speaker, that won't work. So what will? I have a few suggestions. First, we must clearly identify the basic components of new industrial and scientific policies that will help us achieve our objectives. Second, we must provide leadership and the political will to achieve those objectives. How?
First, create an economic co-ordination and development board for the Montreal region: get all economic sectors together; define common objectives.
June 4, 1991

Second, create a cabinet committee responsible for the economic recovery of Montreal and the region.
Third, encourage the creation in Montreal of a consortium of big and small businesses; pools of risk capital; study and technical services; super-incubators.
Fourth, invest selectively but substantially, with research and development as the local point; develop high-tech niches; strengthen the aeronautics sector; scientific research parks; centres of excellence.
Fifth, ensure that Quebec and Montreal receive their fair share of funding for research and development, not the 13 per cent we are getting now.
Sixth, design manpower training and adjustment programs that consider Montreal's objectives for economic diversity. No more one-man shows by this government, Mr. Speaker!
And finally, leadership and political will are the basic prerequisites of this recovery.
I painted a gloomy picture of the current situation. Unfortunately, it is also an accurate picture. The situation in Montreal is as I described it, but I also want to show there is light at the end of the tunnel.
I just offered the House six proposals, six steps for recovery. The government must act now, it must act quickly and it must act on several levels at once. However, to be effective, the types of action taken must be complementary and not compete with each other. The federal government must demonstrate, through a variety of concrete achievements-we have had enough studies-its political will to give Montreal new hope for the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed the hon. member's speech, primarily because he is the first who spoke today to come out with some positive suggestions. Everybody else got up and complained and moaned and groaned.
I am concerned about some of his suggestions, not all of them, and to this end I would like him to comment on them.
He is asking the federal government in many ways here to get extremely involved in one city, to have a
Supply
cabinet committee, I think one of his suggestions was, for one city in this country. First, if the hon. member really means this, is he saying then that the federal government should become more directly involved in individual communities throughout this country?
Second, should we take a city and designate it the research centre for Canada or the specific area for certain whatever it may be?
How does that coincide with diversifying the economy of the west, for example, or diversifying the economy of the maritimes, and so on?
Is he suggesting that we have a cabinet committee on Halifax, St. John's and so on so that we could get involved in economic development in those cities? I understand his whole theme but I am not sure why he wants to involve the federal government so directly in the goings on of one city.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his interest and I thank him quite honestly as a representative of a city other than Montreal for the interest that he is showing in my city.
As you look at economic development you realize very quickly that it flows from major motors. There are locomotives. This is true in most of our major cities in terms of the hinterland and the periphery that is around.
Montreal is undoubtedly the major economic locomotive for the province of Quebec. As Montreal goes, so goes the province. There is no doubt about that. That is clear in terms of the development of almost any great city in relationship to the surrounding area anywhere in the world.
The sheer absolute number of unemployed in Montreal is greater than in a great number of the other regions of Canada which really do have a specific economic focus.
What I would say to the minister in response to his question is that if what you want to do is develop economic growth, you have to have regional development, you have to focus on the country as a whole and you cannot neglect your major motors.
The multiplier effect from those major motors is such that it is worthy of having a cabinet committee look at it, specifically at Montreal because of its importance in eastern Canada and in the province of Quebec.

The hon. member for LaSalle-Emard, as always, does come out with very concrete suggestions. You can agree with them or not, but at least he does have something to offer.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, it is hard to rise in this House to explain the economic situation in Montreal.
I am particularly concerned with the clothing industry in Montreal, simply because our family business, which is apparel retailing, is closely linked to that industry in Montreal. We have been involved in that business since 1912. It has been a while. Throughout the years, we have met clothing manufacturers from Montreal, but these last few years, we noticed that the industiy, once a major industry in Montreal, is going downhill. That is a serious cause of concern for people whose livelihood depends on the clothing industry.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to give you a short history of that industry. At one point, a few years back, Montreal's clothing industry was booming. As the main clothing manufacturer in North America, Montreal was second only to New York City. It was a major industry in this country, and it was flourishing. I remember when Montreal's clothing industry was extremely busy in the mid-50s.
When we think that all across Canada, about 120,000 people used to earn a living working in the clothing industry and 57 per cent of those jobs were in Montreal. And that, Mr. Speaker, does not include another 20,000 people or so who were working at home. There were also some plants in the Beauce area, outside the Quebec region and there was another group in the eastern part of Quebec. So, it meant 90,000 jobs all across Quebec that were directly associated with the clothing industry.
Of course, one of the things that hurt us was the imports. If we take a look at the numbers-and they tend to increase-about 30 per cent of the clothing is imported and, sadly, that percentage is still increasing.
The federal government certainly failed in that area by not protecting the clothing industry, as it failed in many other areas. You know that much has been said about research and development. But what is still more important than that? It is the development of the existing technology and the implementation of the development. Research in that area is not as necessary as in the past.
June 4, 1991

Another factor that weakens the clothing industry in Montreal is the interest rates. In Montreal, the manufacturers needed to have access to capital, lots of it, in order to maintain their competitiveness. With high interest rates-I am aware of that, because I have been in contact with several organizations, the unions, the Guilds, as we call them, the Dress and Sportwear Manufacturers' Guild-so, they were explaining to me that it was extremely difficult for them to upgrade their equipment because of high interest rates. This is a suggestion that we could make to the federal government, that is to try, with a special program, to help the clothing industry, which is so important to the city of Montreal. If not, we could do as a number of organizations did, like the Canadian Manufacturers's Association, and reduce the interest rates.
However, if it is impossible to do so, we will have to set up a program for the clothing industry because of its importance. In the last year, and in the last months in particular, I was able to note the difficulties faced by the manufacturers in Montreal. Because of the 7 per cent GST they must add to the 8 per cent provincial tax, the clothing retailers whose products were not taxable before must now add 15.5 per cent to the bills they give to their customers. You can see how that has affected the retail sales of clothing in Quebec stores. Consumers found this price increase too hard to absorb and effectively there was a 25 to 30 per cent drop in sales.
Considering all these factors, it is no wonder that the clothing industry had such an important decline. We all know that it used to be a very flourishing industry in Quebec, but we are letting it slip right through our fingers. It is almost criminal to see that we cannot find solutions to the problems encountered by the manufacturers. Yet, they have stated time and time again that they want to meet with the federal and provincial authorities to find a solution for their industry. One must not forget that a great many women were employed in the clothing industry. I must say that, over the years, the average wage in this industry had a fairly normal growth and is now over 9 dollars. It is not much, but there has been over the years a fairly substantial increase.
