Another element that concerned the manufacturing sector in Montreal is free trade. From the outset, they were against the free trade agreement, because they saw the difficulties it could bring to their industry. Now, they raise a cry of alarm. When they see that the central government wants to negotiate a free trade agreement with Mexico, knowing that the hourly wage in Mexico is far lower than ours, even ten times lower. In Montreal, they say: "We hardly had time to adjust.'' It has been very hard for them to adjust to free trade with United States and now we want to plunge them in a free trade with Mexico where the hourly wage is much lower.
So, you can imagine the anxiety prevailing in this sector. What are we asking of the central government? We implore you, this industry is very important to Quebec and to Montreal. You cannot leave this sector, this industry which means a lot to Montreal, at the mercy of free trade with the United States and Mexico. Moreover, interest rates are too high. You must realize that this industry used to be the pillar of the Montreal economy. But if you let it continue to be bloodied by free trade with the United States and Mexico, you will see that we will lose completely an industry that was and still is so important and that can be saved.
So, to wind up, I say to the government: The manufacturing sector in Montreal wants to speak to you, to have the opportunity to express its great concern and to propose alternatives, solutions to save this industry. They speak not only on their behalf but also on behalf of the 90,000 persons who earn their living from an industry which they see disappearing.
So, it cannot be stated more clearly. They want to have the opportunity to speak out and to express their concern.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly interested in the comments of the hon. member for Lasalle-Emard who suggested that Montreal be a high-tech area following along in the aerospace type work that has been done by the takeover by Bombardier of Canadair and the work done on Bill C-22 where we changed the patent law and allowed research and development in pharmaceuticals.

Is it the view of the Liberal Party that we should also be a country of high tariffs where we keep out the manufactured products of other countries, particularly clothing and footwear; that we should be a country where the import of those articles that can clearly be purchased in other countries cheaper be denied our citizens so that they pay higher prices for those articles; and that we allow no trade so our high technology cannot be sold in those other countries?
I was wondering if he could square the economic philosophy of the Liberal Party.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member is making reference to the fact that we import 30 per cent, I never suggested that we should have additional tariffs. All I am saying is that the clothing manufacturing industry in Montreal was extremely important and there is no reason why we have to leave this industry open to the wind and allow it to disappear on us because of either free trade or high interest rates.
Montreal, with regard to the high tech and pharmaceuticals industries-obviously everybody promotes high tech in Montreal or elsewhere, but it does not mean we have to sacrifice a domain where we were once the champions.
All we are saying is if we had decent interest rates, if there was a reasonable amount of dialogue with these people to find alternatives so that they could modernize, we could compete with these imports. However, we seem to have shackled them with high interest rates and all kinds of disadvantages so they are having difficulty competing with the imports. These are artificial difficulties that the government has put on their backs.
We are not trying to trade off high tech for the clothing industry. It was a viable industry, we had the expertise and it was very labour-intensive, especially for women. Why should we sacrifice it when we do not have to? All they need is a little bit of dialogue and understanding and we can balance both of them easily.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member mentioned the free trade debate. Throughout that debate, I sat on the parliamentary committee studying the agreement. Each and every association representing the clothing and textile industries which came forward said they
were against the free trade deal. They also said if the agreement was deemed necessary, we had to have adjustment programs. Now then, the prime minister promised adjustment programs for those grand industries, as recommended by the de Grandpre Commission, the Macdonald Commission and the Economic Council of Canada.
Since the hon. member knows the textile and clothing industries pretty well, can he tell us what adjustment programs have been planned for those industries affected by the Free Trade Agreement. I am not as familiar with those industries as the hon. member is.

Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the answer is no. What is going on here? The Prime Minister and some of his ministers announced a number of programs, but unfortunately, there are none and that is what has us puzzled. Who is telling the truth here?

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to go back briefly to some comments that were made by the hon. member for LaSalle- Emard, when he mentioned that Montreal was the industrial centre of Quebec, and that if Montreal was doing well, industrially speaking, if there was industrial development in Montreal, it was the whole province which was benefitting, and that if Montreal was not developing, it was the province that was hurting.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some comments as a way of explanation in order to tell him that I do not agree entirely with that. I would like that the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard recognize that when there is development in the Quebec regions, whether in the field of natural resources or the development of primary industries, for example, the major aluminum projects in Becancour, Deschambault, Baie Comeau or Sept lies, my hon. colleague should recognize that the engineering firms in Montreal are doing work on those sites. Lavallin and SNC are there. There are also manufacturing
June 4, 1991

industries from the Montreal region which build industrial equipment that go into these new plants. If the forest industry is doing well in Abitibi, in Lac Saint Jean and on the North Shore, again, Mr. Speaker, it is the parts manufacturers, the equipment manufacturers of the Montreal region that benefit from it.
So I would like my colleagues from Montreal to admit that when the federal government takes part in the economic diversification of Quebec regions, Montreal also benefits from it. We should not think that because some Montreal areas are in trouble, the situation is catastrophic in the rest of the province.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I would like to underline that, in his speech, my friend the minister responsible for Montreal Island has described fully the federal government's initiatives in the Montreal region. We could conclude from his comments that this great metropolis is evolving, like other urban centers all over the world, and is about to take a new direction which will allow it to live a new age of prosperity. In fact, we intended pursuing the actions already undertaken to that end, particularly in matters of industrial development.
Historically, industrial development has always been the cornerstone of Montreal's economic prosperity. We just have to remember the many big companies located near Montreal's docks or the other main cross roads of the time. With the evolving means of communication, Montreal's industrial base has had to adapt and we saw the rise of new industries, with a bigger technological content.
While more efficient companies were created in new industrial areas, the more traditional industry also needed attention, in order to cope with international competition.
These are indicative of the two main thrusts of the federal government action to support and revitalize the industry in Montreal: first, rely heavily on the strengths of the Montreal economy and, second, help more traditional businesses still providing many jobs, to update and reinforce the expertise acquired over the past few decades.
When I am through, hon. members of this House will realize that the opposition motion disregards an entire set of measures that have been implemented by the
Supply
government I have the honour to be a member of. As you all know, the Montreal economy is remarkably complex. Nonetheless, this government has managed to sucessfully implement a plan of action in which industrial development plays a major part.
The federal government's strategy is, first, to develop high technology sectors in Montreal, particularly in the following three industries: aeronautics/aerospace, elec-tronics/telecommunications and pharmaceutical industry.
One of the main projects the federal government has carried out in these sectors in years is certainly the establishment of the Canadian Space Agency in the Montreal area. This decision unanimously added a major change in direction to strengthen and give a new start to this industry destined for a great future. Through its activities, the Space Agency has helped strenghen industries in related sectors and, above all, create new businesses attracted by the Space Agency. Furthermore, thanks to its research programs, the Space Agency has helped develop new industries in advanced sectors such as composite materials.
In fact, all parties with a stake in Montreal's economic future agree that the aeronautics industry is one of the city's major strengths. The federal government, through targeted support, has helped to ensure a bright future for this outstanding member of Montreal's industry.
The decision to privatize Canadair gave the internationally known company a second lease on life, as reflected in the recent success of the Challenger. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that not long ago, the Prime Minister helped launch the regional jet, which has caught the interest of a number of airlines, despite an economic climate that is not very conducive to investment.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has provided significant support for research and development by all large companies in the Montreal region. Federal assistance has on untold occasions been instrumental in developing new products by companies that include Pratt & Whitney, Canadair, Spar Aerospace and Heroux. Thanks to federal support, these companies have been able to compete on world markets. The recent launching

June 4, 1991
Supply
by Spar of a communications satellite is an eloquent case in point.
In electronics and telecommunications, many large companies have received federal support to develop new products and thus acquire a substantial share of the North American market. You will recall that Paramax in Montreal won the contract for all the electronics for the frigates, thus generating a significant subcontracting potential for a number of firms located in the Montreal region.

Moreover, it is important to stress the importance of the decision to privatize Teleglobe Canada for the development of a new leadership by the private sector in the field of satellite communications.

I would now like to talk about a sector that our government, by way of a courageous decision, has helped revitalize. All the members will remember that the pharmaceutical industry was once a major industry in the Montreal area. Indeed, one only had to drive along the TransCanada highway, between the Decarie expressway and Vaudreuil, to see the numerous pharmaceutical companies along this important stretch of highway.
The members of the House have often heard debates and speeches emphasizing the importance of putting a stop to the stagnation of that industry, a process which has started in the early 80's. The pharmaceutical companies had drastically reduced their investments in research and development because the results of their basic research were no longer protected.
The changes that we made to the Patent Act enabled us to completely reverse the situation. Indeed, without government aid of any kind, several big companies decided to invest in R&D, as well as to expand their research centers in Montreal, among others Merck Frosst, and Nordic laboratories.
Even though the Montreal region experiences problems that essentially arise out of certain economic conditions, that city possesses nevertheless many of the characteristics of a winner. The cities that attract businesses and companies all have something in common. In
each of them the political and business leaders have cooperated to create a favourable environment for development. The leadership shown by the private sector is also particularly noticeable in those cities. By the way, the federal government supported a private sector initiative by helping with the establishment of a high technology park in the Montreal region. The interested firms will thus be able to concentrate their resources in an environment conducive to this high level activity.
The technology park will, in fact, act as a catalyst to improve liaison between universities, government research centres and business. This linkage between universities and business will have top priority in industrial sectors that the world over are the foundation of a flourishing industry: aeronautics, biotechnology, microelectronics and informatics.
Although federal support has tended to concentrate on the most advanced and most promising sectors, we have also included other industries that have always played an important role in to Montreal. For instance, the transportation equipment industry registered major investments in recent years that would have been impossible without direct government intervention. A recent announcement that Dowty would invest $90 million to manufacture landing gears has further consolidated Montreal's position as a major centre for aeronautics. In the automobile industry, Montupet has now located in the Montreal region to manufacture automobile parts, while 3,000 jobs were saved at Ste-Therese thanks to federal intervention. Without our support, the GM plant at Ste-Therese would now probably be a thing of the past.
I would now like consider another aspect of our integrated program for supporting industrial development in Montreal. As I said earlier, the Montreal area has always had a very diversified industrial structure, whose sectors have had their ups and downs, owing to various factors. With increased international competition has come the need to adjust to a new game plan. The free trade agreement has made it very important to help businesses update their plant, to be able to face the competition.
June 4, 1991

Bearing this in mind, our government designed a program that was tailored to meet the new challenge of a global market. The Manufacturing Productivity Improvement Program, which was an instant success, has now been in place for two and a half years. To be eligible for this program, businesses must meet very strict criteria. Nevertheless, the results have been most impressive. The program has received 250 applications for assistance, and sixty businesses have been able to benefit from government assistance, thanks to contributions totalling $14 million.
Similarly, it seemed important to us to get small businesses into new product lines. Just a few months ago, the minister responsible for Economic and Regional Development announced the creation of an innovation assistance program with a $3 million enveloppe. This program is only six months old, but over 30 requests have already been received and over half a million dollars in contributions. It is indeed off to a good start.
I would like, in closing, to mention two initiatives we are particularly proud of, which were very well received by the communities concerned. Over the years, some industries congregated in specific areas of Montreal had been deteriorating gradually. This was particularly true of eastern and southwestern Montreal. To overcome that situation, the Canadian government agreed to implement two programs suited to the needs of these disadvantaged areas.
In February 1988, minister Robert de Cotret announced the implementation of the Industrial Recovery Program for East Montreal (IRPEM). With a $35 million budget, this program resulted from the Picard report and the work of the Committee for the Economic Recovery and Revitalization of Employment in East-End Montreal. The IRPEM is designed to strenghten the local industrial structure, encourage the industrial diversification of that area and foster the establishment and development of new businesses, particularly small- and medium-sized businesses. The latest statistics show that the minister responsible for implementing this program had received 326 requests and that over $28 million had been spent to support recovery in this area of Montreal.
In May 1990, my colleague, minister Benoit Bouchard, announced a similar program for the south-western part of Montreal, the IRPSWM.
This program is intended to provide assistance for the design and construction of new facilities as well as for the extension and modernization of existing facilities.
Supply
This all new program has already resulted in investments of almost $9 million.
A close look at federal government actions reveal that due to its flexibility our strategy fits the various capabilities offered by greater Montreal that were identified in the Picard report. This flexibility is particularly obvious in the case of industrial development, where we have put in place programs on a needs basis. In fact, that is the strategy we intend to follow in the months to come because we are convinced it is the best way to develop Montreal's potential while allowing the private sector to participate fully.

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that regional development is crucial for the province of Quebec and for Canada. There is no doubt either that the entrepreneurial skills of Quebecers have their roots in the Beauce area, in Lac Saint-Jean, in the Eastern townships and in the Abitibi. That is why I absolutely cannot understand the fact that this government is abandoning the Gaspe and the Northshore regions. I cannot understand, for instance, his reluctance to push for flow-through shares, which are so important for the mining industry.
That being said, one must recognize that when the unemployment rate exceeds 15 per cent, as is the case in Montreal, you have a number of unemployed workers that far exceeds that of many regions of Canada. Montreal is the heart of the economy in Quebec. My question is this: Does the hon. member, the parliamentary secretary, think that Quebec, as a province, can possibly win if Montreal loses?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very easy to answer the question asked by my honourable colleague from LaSalle-Emard. It is obvious that if the industrial structure of Montreal becomes more diversified, if the federal, provincial and municipal levels of government work together to attract new industries in Montreal, namely high technology industries which create new jobs, and if development and support programs can help reinforce existing industries, it is obvious that the economy of Montreal will contribute, and I think we agree on that, to the economy of Quebec as a province. But I want the hon. member to know that I find it very difficult to let someone claim that Montreal is the only place that counts in Quebec. The hon. member should look at the reality. The regions contribute to the development of Montreal in the same

June 4, 1991

way that Montreal can provide expertise and specialized services for the development of the regions.
My honourable colleague claims that the federal government, that is the Progressive Conservative Party, has abandoned the Northshore and Gaspe regions in Quebec, but I would like to remind him that, since 1984, there have been more industrial investments on the Northshore, from Tadoussac to Havre-Saint-Pierre, then in the 25 years previous to that. Indeed, Reynolds, Quebec and Ontario Paper in Baie-Comeau, as well as Alouette in Sept-Iles, have all benefited from federal investments. Moreover, other investments in the private sector will also be announced shortly, thanks to the direct intervention of the federal government, through his regional development programs.
As regard the Gaspesie, some of our colleagues were in Gaspe last week to announce three important initiatives that will enable the Gaspe peninsula to benefit from industrial development as well as economic diversification based on initiatives taken by local people and entrepreneurs. Mr. Speaker, that is what we call a sound intervention in the field of regional development, and our government has been acting in that fashion since 1984, in Montreal as well as in the regions of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I have had the pleasure to sit with my hon. friend on The Province of Quebec Chamber of Commerce. At the time, it seemed to me that the performance of a governement could be judged by its results. Well, the results that we can see in Quebec now are not very glorious for the party in office. In Montreal, the unemployment rate is 15 per cent. In Quebec remote areas, it can go up to 20 per cent, not taking into account the people who outlast their unemployment benefit period and are now on welfare.
I remember, a few years back, when I was working pretty hard to get the Space Agency on the South Shore. We got the Space Agency, we were proud and boastful, and we kept repeating: "Now, we have the Space Agency.'' Time has gone by, but the Space Agency is not yet built. There might be a hundred employees in Montreal. At the same time, we launched the centres of
excellence, and the University of Calgary obtained the contract for space research, while the Prime Minister said that aerospace research and development would take place in Montreal. We realize today that Pratt and Whitney has put nearly 1000 employees on unemployment.
Imagine, we boasted because we got the Space Agency, and I was so proud at the time. But there was no serious basis to all that. This plan to develop aerospace in the Montreal area, it was old rubbish. We realize today that approximatly 800 aerospace jobs have disappeared in the Montreal region, and that is counting only those at Pratt and Whitney, and the Space Agency.
The hon. member who has just delivered his speech is boasting about the help that the federal government has given Quebec. The fact is the federal government simply helps us pay for welfare and unemployment. It certainly is of no assistance to us in terms of economic development.

I would like to assure my colleague from the South Shore riding of Montreal that the Quebec caucus follows very closely the actions taken by the
June 4. 1991

government for the economic development of Montreal, and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the hon. member for Manicouagan who praised the government for what it has done in the last few years, and who quoted several figures. However, there are figures he forgot to mention. In this regard, I would like to point out to him that this debate, today, is about the unemployed in Montreal. speechtext:

had tremendous difficulties at the end of the seventies and into the eighties. People had to leave their homes to find work somewhere else, but now, they are coming back, and I am very happy about it.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate with the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Cartierville.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask my colleague for Manicouagan to what jobs he is referring?
I rise today to spotlight the poor state of the Montreal region. This sad situation is due in good part to initiatives like the GST, as well as to a lack of initiatives like job creation, which was promised by the Conservative Government.
In Quebec, nearly 5,000 companies and 14,000 individuals have been forced into bankruptcy in 1990. Most of these cases were in Montreal. The level of unemployment is more than 14 per cent in Montreal and rises to 25 per cent east of Montreal; there are also those on welfare. The unemployment rate does not seem to be getting any lower. All those jobs could be lost forever.
Plants closings, commercial and personal bankruptcies, relocations do not bode well for the future. All these Quebecers who suddenly lose their jobs and are without hope of getting them back must rely on the unemployment insurance for their rent. How many of them will be forced to go on welfare?
According to action unemployed, the cuts and changes made to the unemployment insurance program have really hurt. In Quebec city, the situation is all the more serious since it is a region where employment is seasonal. Many peoples have to had to go on the dole, following the changes introduced by Bill C-21.
And what about immigrants? When a company must cut jobs, the first to go are very often the last ones hired, and most of the time, they are immigrants. Some welcome!
Mr. Speaker, Montreal has enormous potential but this government and its irresponsible department seem determined to check its development.

June 4, 1991
Supply
The GST is but one initiative affecting everyone and reducing consumer spending. When sales are down, so is spending and employees must be laid off. As a result, unemployment is sky high and welfare offices are sending an increasing number of cheques.
Montreal already has 14 per cent of its population who depend on welfare to survive and there seems to be no economic recovery in sight.
Food banks find it more and more difficult to help soup kitchens. Demand is rising instead of diminishing, it seems. It is not healthy to start the day on an empty stomach.
As for children, they cannot be expected to learn and retain what they are taught in school if they do not eat properly. That is not how they can be able to develop their potential and be alert.
I would like to cite a few facts on welfare and UIC in Montreal to give a better perspective to this problem.
Between March 1990 and March 1991, 65,400 jobs were lost, of which 17,500 were in the clothing industry, and 14,300 were in hotels and restaurant service industries.
The maximum amount of benefits a person could receive from UI was $480 a week. The welfare benefit being paid to a single person willing to participate in special government make-work programs is $587 per month and $486 per month if they are not willing to participate in these programs.
With this type of revenue, it is a miracle that anyone can survive in our society.

Mr. Speaker, a society which cannot meet the basic needs of its citizens, making them completely dependent on the State, not by choice but out of necessity, is a society doomed to face a depression.
It is difficult to be optimistic, to create attainable dreams, to give growing children a vision of a better future when, as parents, the daily worries are as real as the rent payment which often takes more than 50 per cent of their meager income. How is it possible to give children nourishing meals and proper clothing when work becomes more and more scarce and is often limited to short periods?
Mr. Speaker, Montreal was, not so long ago, a major city where life was good. Today it holds the national record for bank robberies. It has a waiting list of 22,000
families who want low rental housing and 40 per cent of its people would need this type of housing.

When the federal government, which through the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation was the main builder of subsidized housing in Canada, dropped its rental renovation program two years ago and in its recent budget announced cuts to social housing, it did nothing to remedy the situation.
The country is in crisis and Montreal seems to be going downhill at a very rapid rate. Without basic security like housing and food, how can people be expected to be in top shape, ready to learn new skills, on minimum revenues given by UIC, that could be out of date by the time the courses are finished.

Mr. Speaker, this is the early 90s and the future does look kind of gloomy for the Montreal residents. Crime and violence are on the rise, the cost of living is becoming more and more prohibitive for too many families, low-cost housing is rare and jobs are obsolete.
Since coming into office, this government has done nothing but overtax people, and they still do not understand why people cannot make ends meet!
Mr. Speaker, this government has no consideration whatsoever for the wellfare of Canadian men and women, who will take the opportunity, at the next election, to remind them of their existence.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I have to remind the House that when I put questions to the minister responsible for the Montreal area, he answers by wondering how I can be so bold as to mention these issues That is on record, it is published in Hansard. As far as I am concerned, that is unacceptable, and a government which is so bold as to keep a minister who gives little hope to the Montreal residents and does not care about them, does not deserve to govern this country.

June 4, 1991

Mr. Crow, appearing before the Committee of Finance, told us that it was absolutely necessary to increase interest rates to curb inflation, I replied to him that he was doing everything to create a recession. I was right to tell Mr. Crow that he was creating one. You know, I have been in business for more than 15 years. Bankruptcies are thus in fact created. I do not have the exact figure in mind, but we know there are bankruptcies in numbers large enough to realize how bad the situation is now, particularly in Montreal. The blame lies with this government which does not know how to manage economic growth. It is not by giving money, from time to time to this or that businesss, to show that you are doing something, that you control the economic system while having a stable economic system, a reasonable growth. That is not what has been done during the last few years. So, it is a shame to see these people who worked so hard be penniless again and without a job. These are entrepreneurs who had built firms and are now jobless. It's not only them, but all their employees who find themselves unemployed.

When these people end up without a job, the spouse often says: "You're no good, you can't find a job, what's wrong with you?" Then the two start arguing and end up getting divorced. Then there is a problem with the children, with the families. It's a terrible social problem and we must be aware of it. It seems that this government is not aware of it. It is breaking up families and destroying the whole society and it will take 10 to 15 years to correct. That is where

the misfortune of Montreal lies presently, there is a lot of unemployment and many people on social welfare.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take part in this opposition day debate on the motion proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace. I would like to read the motion before commenting on it, because what it says is important.
That this House condemns the government for having abandoned the population of Montreal through its obvious lack of political will to provide jobs and economic opportunities to the people of this region.
Mr. Speaker, we have all accepted voluntarily to take ten minutes to speak to this question because we believe, as liberal members representing the region of fyfontreal, that it is very important. I have three points to make. When I say we have to give the opportunity to the people of Montreal to create jobs, to find jobs, I am not saying that the government should intervene everywhere. But, as politicians, we have the duty to create opportunities. As for the monetary policy, everybody agrees, in Quebec particularly, that this government's monetary policy is an incredible economic disaster. We cannot have a free-trade agreement with the United States and let our dollar go up while we implement this agreement. Because we automatically lose all the advantages that we had. Canada gave itself a social structure and priorized it and the human values going with it compared to the american economy having a totally different structure. By letting our dollar go up, we lose the little competitive edge that we had.

June 4, 1991

What is worse is that we have seen this government, through the Governor of the Bank of Canada, increase each week the interest rates and make the situation unbearable. We have then a high dollar and high interest rates. Mr. Speaker, we know that every company has a line of credit today. If interest rates go up, interest charges take up a larger portion of the operating budget.
Those are major policies which were disastrous for the economy, and that was a choice, Mr. Speaker. It was not due to international circumstances. The recession we are presently going through in Canada is a Canadian-made recession, triggered by the economic policies of this government. That is what we want to say in our motion today. The words are very clear. They relate specifically to the political will to provide jobs and economic opportunities for the people of that region. And then, how many times did the Quebec government, the Cornell du patronat, all the social and economic interest groups of the Montreal region and the whole province of Quebec say: "We call on the Conservative government in Ottawa to stop its high interest rates and high Canadian dollar policies because they are disastrous for our economy. We are not competitive on the American market"? During the electoral campaign in 1988, the Conservatives led everyone to believe that their policy would aim for a stable economic situation. We must admit that Quebec subscribed to that theory. It is the province of Quebec, especially Montreal, that pays the price for this same free trade policy, a policy that was not followed by an adequate monetary policy aimed at responding to the impact of the Free Trade Agreement.
When we say that this government has no policy, the evidence is there. One does not need to be a genius or some expert in economic or international affairs to see it. A dollar too high, plus high interest rates-
The high interest rates of 1982.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

So, we have to compare with the rest of the world.
When interest rates are high in Canada, but high also in the United States, we are competitive, as problems are the same on both sides of the border. However, when we create our own problems- Here, Mr. Speaker, I just woke up the Conservatives. That's it, I woke them up.
They are shocked by the truth.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
No doubt about it. What I was saying when my friend interrupted is that we had high interest rates, a high dollar and, on top of that, Mr. Speaker, the famous GST. This government said that it had to slow down the economy, that Canadians were spending too much and that was creating inflation. To that end it raised the interest rates, to prevent Canadians from spending. Then there was the new tax on goods and services applied to everything.
When we talk about inflation, we should not forget the taxes. Everything we pay to governments are taxes, whether they are federal taxes, provincial taxes, municipal taxes, school taxes, building permits, licence plates, etc. If we add all these taxes-and they keep increasing-we see what is responsible for the rise in inflation.
On the one hand, the government tried to control inflation with the interest rates, but on the other, it imposed the GST. Now we see the result. The inflation rate rose from 4 to 6 per cent. So, this government does not know exactly what it is doing. On the one hand, it says that it wants to reduce inflation, but on the other, it increases taxes.
Mr. Speaker, these words are not mine. The government members will deny it. This morning, I heard the minister responsible for the Montreal area say that the Liberals were to blame, after seven years of conservative rule.
But Mr. Speaker, these words are not mine. Let me quote from an article I read:

"One in four Montrealers lives in poverty, starving. City population getting older and poorer, Health department finds. Montreal's population is growing older and poorer and one in four of the city's residents is below the poverty line." It is not new, says The Gazette on April 18, 1990.
June 4, 1991

Yesterday, we heard about an important study on
taxes.

"Tax up SI,530 a year during Tory rule."

Because of this government's policies since 1984, a family today pays $1,530 more in taxes than it did in 1984.
In 1984, the Conservatives were in power, not the Liberals. So if they want to blame someone, they should start with themselves, especially considering that from month to month, they have remained steady at 14 per cent in the polls because people have finally understood.
More news: a 70 per cent increase in bankruptcies in April; in Quebec, 2,097 bankruptcies were filed in April 1991, 72 per cent more than April last year.
Earlier, I heard the parliamentary secretary talking about government policies, and he said that everything was fine. Mr. Speaker, this is our twentieth National Environment Week. Environment Canada's Green Plan has a budget of $3 billion and urges Canadians to play a role, both individually and as a group, in cleaning up and protecting their environment. Some of the Green Plan's initiatives have already started across this country. The Canadian government has announced programs to clean up the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence. June 4, 1991
Furthermore, an unprecedented air quality agreement was signed with the United States to deal with the problem of acid rain and other types of trans-border air pollution.

Mr. Speaker, on March 31, the federal-provincial forest agreement between Nova Scotia and the federal government expired. Both governments have been dragging their feet and have not yet renewed the agreement. Concerns have also been expressed that a new agreement must be signed for longer than the previous two-year bridging period. The government should get on with it and sign an agreement immediately.

Mr. Speaker, in last week's debate over Bill C-5, an act to amend the Aeronautics Act and to amend an act to amend the Aeronautics Act, discussion about Lester B. Pearson International Airport and the effects on surrounding communities was once again front and centre.
My constituents and I appreciate the co-operation that is being shown by all sides of the House in encouraging the speedy passage of this legislation.
However, my constituents and I wish to make clear certain misconceptions that were presented by the opposition.
Residents who live in the communities surrounding the airport are being presented as airport haters unable to tolerate disturbance of any kind. At best this is an
oversimplification of the position my constituents have about Pearson. At worst the proliferation of this misconception means we jeopardize our ability to work toward a rewarding partnership between the airport and its surrounding communities.
My constituents wish it to be known that they appreciate the benefits the airport can provide and that, as long as the airport plays fair and accepts its responsibility toward the community, they will work with the airport to foster a productive and equally beneficial relationship.

Mr. Speaker, last week a very sad incident occurred in Winnipeg. We watched on national news as a young Indian man asked for justice and understanding from the Canadian people and their governments on Winnipeg's radio airwaves.
Mr. Cameron Kerley Antoine was sent out of the province of Manitoba as a young child to the United States where he was adopted by a non-Indian bachelor. He was beaten and sexually abused by his adoptive father for years until he killed him. Originally sentenced to 15 years to life, this sentence was reduced in 1986 to 20 years on compassionate grounds by the Governor of Kansas.
Now serving his sentence in Canada, Mr. Kerley Antoine deserves compassion from the Canadian government.
I urge the government to review his incarceration in light of his own victimization, in light of some previous acquittals of victims of spousal violence who killed their spouses, and in light of the years he has already served in prison.

Mr. Speaker, this House, and the media were filled yesterday with charges that the Conservative government had increased middle-class taxes dramatically.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is essentially right, but as the author of the report stated on The Journal last night, if the Conservatives had not inherited a huge debt, right now the government would have a multi-billion dollar surplus.
June 4, 1991

However, while high taxes may be understandable, governments at all levels could be doing a better job in treating taxpayers. There ought to be more co-operation between various levels of governments so overlap and duplication are eliminated, so we can work toward the integration of local, provincial and federal taxes, so tax forms can be simplified, so taxpayers can see exactly how much taxes they pay and so that we can put an end to hidden taxes.
I hope the Economic Council of Canada can explore these areas as it conducts the Prime Minister's study on competitiveness. I hope we can achieve what is really needed, a total reform of the tax system.

Mr. Speaker, as the dust from this government's budget of last February begins to settle, the ramifications of the government's lack of commitment to education and health are beginning to be felt by Canadians from coast to coast.
According to the president of the Canadian Medical Association, Dr. Lavoie, Canada's medicare system will be in ruins within the next 10 years if this government continues its present policies.
In my province of Prince Edward Island, the $2.3 billion cut in provincial transfer payments is now affecting the ability of the province and the hospitals themselves to maintain their health care services.
Queen Elizabeth Hospital will be closing 25 per cent of its beds for the month of July and 22 beds for the rest of the year. Our other main hospital, Prince County, will be closing almost 10 per cent of its beds for the rest of the year.
The other hospitals in my province are being affected as well.
I urge the federal government to recognize how the policies arc hurting Canadians and to rectify the damage it has done to our health care system.

Mr. Speaker, how are we going to resolve the fundamental conflict that haunts our country, a conflict between two very different visions of Canada: the equality of all versus the distinct society?
In 1867 we found the answer by adopting a federal rather than a unitary system of government. In 1991 we may find the answer by giving every province exclusive jurisdiction over language, culture and communications. Language rights would be attached to places and not to people. This would give Quebec full control over matters it considers essential for its survival. It would also give the nine other provinces the right to have unilingual traffic tickets or cereal boxes if they wished. That could substantially reduce the support for Quebec independence and allow other differences to be settled by common sense rather than by emotion.

Mr. Speaker, Amnesty International's detailed report today begins: "Nearly two years after the suppression of peaceful pro-democracy protests, which resulted in the massacre of hundreds of civilians in Beijing on June 4, 1989, human rights violations continue to be widespread in China".
China refuses to answer inquiries by Amnesty or by members of this Parliament, arguing that human rights are internal matters only.
Nevertheless, since China shares international trade and credit and responsibility for the U.S. led UN invasion of Iraq, China cannot ignore the UN declaration of human rights. Although it upholds the right to work and fair pay, to health care and to education, it must also uphold the rights to life, liberty and security of person, to freedom of peaceful assembly, and to being presumed innocent until proved guilty in a lawful public trial.

June 4, 1991

Mr. Speaker, as we begin Environment Week in Canada, I would like to bring to the attention of the House the most important anniversary we will be celebrating this time next year, namely the 20th anniversary of the Stockhom Conference on the Environment. At that time, heads of stale will have gathered in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, for the June 1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development.
Mr. Speaker, we are proud of the spirit of consultation Canada has displayed on the international scene. We recognize the need for Canada and the other industrialized nations to help developing countries meet their needs for sustainable growth.
All Canadians will benefit from Canada achieving its goals and contributing to setting a new course worldwide. So, they can start by setting an example at home. During Environment Week, I encourage everyone to make a special effort to preserve and clean up the environment. Let us all be active partners in this nation-wide endeavour. The future of Canada depends on it!

Hun. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, the people of Scoudouc, in my riding of Beauscjour, have just sustained a loss they would rather have been spared. The fact is that Canada Post has decided to dose their post office. This decision came as a surprise to everyone.
In the letter announcing the closure, Canada Post refers to communications between municipal authorities. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that had the corporation been in touch with the president of the local service district of Scoudouc and myself, there would still be a post office in Scoudouc.
The post office played a major role in the economy of this community. All the businesses established in the industrial park as well as the people of Scoudouc use this local service and they want to keep on using it. So, I urge Canada Post to reconsider and to keep the very busy post office of Scoudouc open.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the volunteer members of the community transitional board for Amherst Aerospace who are working diligently and tirelessly in the interests of securing a lasting future for this major employer in Cumberland county.
This board is made up of volunteer professionals from the area working closely with members of the staff and the union in an effort to protect one of the area's largest employers. The board was formed when it became clear that the owners and financiers of the business had lost interest in the business at a time when in fact it needed the total attention of all concerned.
The board has worked seven days a week since its inception and has been successful in identifying future prospective owners and determining the actions required to make the business viable.
Part of the goal has been to secure community ownership interest, and the board has already been successful in raising a substantial amount of money. The problems are not solved yet. However, this board and its actions are examples of how a community can pull together when given a challenge, and they are to be commended for it.

Mr. Speaker, many Canadian men and women are committed to promoting, through their actions, the fundamental values of our society.
Yesterday, 21 individuals and 4 organizations were honoured during a special ceremony in recognition of their remarkable contribution to communities across the country and received the Citation for Citizenship which is awarded every year.
All over the country, Canadian men and women are working behind the scenes towards a better and fairer future. I think that the energy, determination and
June 4, 1991

dedication of these individuals are what make changes happen. To recognize their work and their contribution to the Canadian society is truly an honour and a pleasure for a government.
Liberty, justice, equality and respect for diversity will continue to prevail in this country as long as we believe in these values and all work for them.
Let us applaud the winners of the Citation for Citizenship who have demonstrated an examplary commitment in promoting the values that Canadian citizenship stands for.

Mr. Speaker, for over 30 years, Quebecers have been demanding the political autonomy they need to grow.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):

In the February budget the Minister of Finance made a commitment that he would review all transfer programs to provinces, in co-operation with the provinces. That commitment is being kept. We are looking at that to ensure that the very good medicare system that we have in this country is sustained. That is one of the reasons for this, but we are looking at all transfer payments, including post-secondary education and social services, to ensure that we have the best system in this country, to maintain it and to make it even better.

Mr. Speaker, if the government wants to ensure that we have the best system, restore the federal funding and we will have the best system.
I would suggest that the Prime Minister ask the people of Newfoundland, where they have had 20 per cent of their acute care beds cut back in health care, where 300 nurses have been laid off; in Nova Scotia, where funding for nursing homes is being cut, and in New Brunswick, where funding is being rolled back. That is where health care really counts, right there in the communities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party asked whether the discussions on the Constitution would deal with Canadian values. I think all of us recognize that in a country like ours, at a time like this, one cannot consider a constitution without dealing with the basic values of this country.
I personally think that would be a very useful dimension to the discussions which we have to undertake. She has made specific reference to a social charter and, naturally, we are prepared to consider her proposals for a social charter and, indeed, consider other constructive proposals by others in this House and in the country.
As the Prime Minister has made clear, while we have a duty which we intend to carry out to put forward specific proposals and clear options for constitutional change, we certainly anticipate that there will be amendments in the process because we do not want to have a situation which has either a closed process or results in closed minds on basic questions that the country has to deal with.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to hear that the government is considering a social charter. I think it is a very important part of what will form the foundation of our country. At the same time it is necessary to have funding for the essential services.
Mr. Speaker, my question is again directed to the Prime Minister. The government's cutbacks in medicare have led to user fees and deterrent fees.
Last April, the minister responsible for National Health and Welfare at the time stated that user fees were a concept that deserved consideration. My question to the Prime Minister is this: Does he endorse user fees? And if not, how does he intend to stop this trend?

Mr. Speaker, the user fee issue was raised, if I am not mistaken, by the Quebec Minister of Social Affairs. The Minister of National Health and Welfare responded several days or several weeks later.
In fact, we are all in favour of having the most advanced, most modem and most generous medicare plan in the world. However, we have to pay for it. We will have to find the money, and that money comes from Canadian taxpayers. The NDP is asking us to lower taxes, but on the other hand, it is also asking us to upgrade services. You can't have both. The two will have to be reconciled at the national level and in the hon. member's mind as well.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. It concerns the government's failure to reach an agreement with the United States to stop polluting the Great Lakes.
After months of delays and stalling by Canada, the Americans finally gave up on this government and announced their own action plan to stop poisoning the Great Lakes.
Why did the government back out of an agreement with the States to finally do something about cleaning up the Great Lakes?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment

Mr. Speaker, as I think most hon. members in this House know, the Canadian government has been working very closely with the American government and with the appropriate provincial and municipal governments, going back as far as 1972, to ensure that good progress is being made with respect to the clean up of the Great Lakes.
The problem, of course, is an immense one. It is a type of problem which has been accumulating in Canada and the Great Lakes as a result of economic activity for decades and decades. Anyone in this House or anyone in the country who thinks that the messes of the past can be cleaned up overnight is wrong.
I think we have made good progress. Most recently, as you know, Mr. Speaker, because you follow these issues very closely, we announced the establishment not so long ago of a $25 million Great Lakes Action Program. I think it is well under way to determining a pollution centre to be established.
We on this side of the House understand that there are no quick fixes to problems which have been building for decades and decades, but we as a government are very committed to ensuring that we proceed thoroughly and in an efficient manner to make sure that the problem is addressed now and in the future.

June 4, 1991
Oral Questions

Why did the government let its own instrument on the Great Lakes, its agreement with Ontario, lapse in March? Why has it done absolutely nothing to get a new agreement and get some action going again?

Point of Order

It is an excellent feature of our parliament, and while we have much to learn from other governmental systems, the question period is one area in which we are in the forefront of the responsible government, and every effort must be made to preserve the excellence of this practice.

Quoting Mr. Jerome is appropriate. I wish he would have quoted him completely and I wish we would return to that practice.
If Question Period were just the seeking of information, there might be some validity to the suggestion that backbenchers in the government have other opportunities. Question Period is the opportunity for making representations on behalf of constituents. The hon. House leader of the New Democratic Party will recognize that caucus is an inappropriate mechanism and is unfair in terms of backbenchers.
Again, the issue is not how long Question Period is, the issue is how fair Question Period is.
It has been suggested in the past by the House leader of the Liberal Party and by the House leader of the New Democratic Party that perhaps we need changes. I would welcome their active participation in the House committee on management so that we can incorporate the rules that Mr. Justice Jerome talked about, quite properly, and maybe we can make them the practice in this House as they have been in the past. We could have more than enough time for members on our side as well as for members on that side to have a fair and even chance. Perhaps we can do it in a way that is free of some of the excessive partisanship, the shouting, the screaming, the accusations and so on which bring this whole institution in disrepute to those who are watching.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will begin with the RRAP, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. That program was designed to help owners renovate houses without rent increases, so we could have more rental units for low-income people.
That program was funded by all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. The federal government, under the previous Minister of Finance, cut funding under that program, and the provincial government followed suit. So, what is left of Montreal's municipal program is not enough, of course, and there is a serious housing problem in that city, specially with regard to low-cost housing.
Montreal was affected by the elimination of the RRAP because it was the only city which participated financially in that program. It is also a city where there were a lot of old apartments in need of repairs, particularly in the south-centre area and the east area.
So, if there is one city that was penalized when the Minister of Finance decided to eliminate that program, it is Montreal.
The POWA is another program that was cancelled. It was designed to help older workers who were losing their jobs because of plant closures in the shoe and clothing industry. That program was reintroduced in a different form, and that is where the problem comes from, Mr. Speaker.
The Program for Older Worker Adjusment must help older workers. In this particular case, namely the Montreal region-and I am pleased that the Minister of Transport, who implemented this program, is with us today-there is a rule according to which there must generally be more than 100 employees in a region of
500,000	people. It goes without saying that Montreal has
a population in the millions, but the problem has to do with the fact that the majority of businesses that shut down employ less than 100 people, and that is where the problem lies for the majority of workers over 55 years of age who have worked in the industry for a number of years. Those people are therefore penalized. They receive no benefit through the POWA program. I do not want to make this a partisan issue, but I am confronted with this problem in my riding of Saint-Leonard and I am convinced that the hon. member for Saint-Denis also faces the same problem. Every day, there are constituents that urge us to change the regulations. I have submitted petitions to the House, among which 5,000 signatures from my riding alone, to have that section modified, because here in Canada, there are large as well as small businesses. When we talk about a minimum of 100 jobs, that means that only a few factories would qualified under that program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this debate today.
Some might wonder why a member from the mari-times would wish to participate in a debate on Montreal. The problems that are raised by my hon. friends opposite are not dissimilar to the ones we have in Atlantic Canada.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace for bringing forward this issue with respect to the economic problems and unemployment in Montreal. However, I must confess that-notwithstanding the fact that he has devoted many, many years of service to the people of NDG and, indeed, to the city of Montreal-I really believe his motion, in which he suggested the government had abandoned the population through the obvious lack of political will to provide jobs and economic opportunities, et cetera, is quite misguided.
What he really means is that he regrets the government has not been sufficiently irresponsible as to spend endless amounts of money to create make-work jobs in the city of Montreal or anywhere else. What the motion says to me is that there is really a philosophical difference between this government and the government of which the hon. member was a very distinguished minis-
June 4, 1991

ter. This government is governing fiscally more responsibly than that which preceded it.
This government believes that the secret to prosperity is through economic strength. Indeed, what we have realized is the fact that the world is changing. Canada could bury its head in the sand and pretend that the world is not out there, or we can get with it. We can attempt to get on board with the economic changes that are happening, the changes in the global world and the economic interdependence of the various countries of the world. Canada is either going to be a part of that or is going to hide its head in the sand and miss out on the opportunities for true long-term prosperity, which includes long-term employment.
Look at what is happening with the unification of Germany and how quickly it has happened. Look at what is happening in Europe as we move, not only to 1992, but indeed to the years beyond. I do not believe that Canada can hide from that. I do not believe the solution to that problem is to do what the previous government did and say: "Spend, spend, spend, get everyone back on a payroll. It does not matter if there is a level of productivity associated with that, it does not matter if we have economic growth and change to meet the new demands of the world, but rather that we simply keep everybody on the payroll and we will not worry about who is going to pay the bills".
Unfortunately, we are now the inheritors of the bills left from years and years of that kind of approach.
We built a high standard of living in this country by doing three things. We artificially propped up our economy through tariffs and subsidies, subsidies that we are now paying for, through the interest on the debt. Second, we were able, for many, many years to benefit from our rich natural resources and the exploitation of those resources without necessarily learning to make the most effective use of those resources in terms of value-added activity. Third, as I have implied, we suffer from years of irresponsible governments which simply tried to keep the cycle moving by spending, whether or not we had the money to pay the bills. That has left us with an extraordinary deficit situation from which we are now burdened with a tremendous national debt.
We have to try to get things in line. We have to look to government to show true leadership in assessing our future strengths through accessing markets. That is why

this government has shown such tremendous leaderships in terms of trade policy. It has recognized that if we can have access to the larger markets of the world, it will provide an opportunity for our manufacturing sectors to develop those markets which in turn will create more jobs for Canadians which will be substantive in the long term.
That does not come easy. We get access to the markets but then we also have to improve our own productivity. There is a job to be done at all levels, both in terms of management and indeed of the workers. Productivity is a key and it is critically important.
Perhaps one of the things we need to do is go back to some of the old values, values that I do not hear talked about a great deal in this House. However, they are values basic to life in Atlantic Canada. They are basic to the part of Atlantic Canada that I have the honour to represent in this House. I am talking about values like the belief that a person has to give a day's work if they want a day's pay. I am talking about values like self-reliance. Whatever happened to the day when people felt that if they had a problem it was their problem and they ought to do something? Every time a plant closes in this country people say: "Oh, what is the government going to do about it?" Or they say: "I don't have a job, why doesn't the government find me a job?"
Government has the responsibility to create a climate to assist in times of difficulty, and so on and so forth, but goodness gracious, at what point do we become the masters of our own destiny? At what point do we say that there is an incumbency upon us to be the ones who are prepared to do what we need to do for ourselves, to show initiative, to show energy, to show entrepreneurialism? On the other side that seems to be a dirty word, but on this side it is a very important one.
There is a role for government in achieving this competitiveness, which is the key to economic prosperity for the future. Obviously, as I have mentioned, the government has to provide access to markets through trade agreements. That is what we are doing. We have done that with the free trade agreement. It is not going to yield its effects in 24 hours or 36 hours, but rather is something that gives us the opportunity, which means that the doors are open. Obviously there are going to have to be adjustments in our manufacturing sector because, whether we like it or not, in some aspects we

simply are not competitive. Therefore, we have to move in the directions where we can be competitive.
Wc have to improve our research and development, our science and our technology capabilities, one of the areas where we have fallen down. Government has done its share in many respects, but the private sector has not. The government has to show leadership in encouraging the private sector to do its share with respect to research and development.
Third, we have to develop a highly skilled labour force. This has to be a focus. I was very encouraged by the remarks in the Speech from the Throne and their thrust on literacy and the relationship between skill levels in individuals and their ability to seek and achieve satisfactory employment. That is where this government, in my judgment, has shown excellent leadership.
I recall that the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace was a member of the C-21 committee. He had some reservations about the fact that the thrust of Bill C-21 was that there is a relationship between unemployment and returning fully and properly to the work force so that workers have the skills that enable them to do more than simply get a job that will tide them through to the next unemployment period, so they can find longterm opportunities, opportunities that will come as a result of the competitiveness approach of this government.
Of course, government has to create a good climate for business. It has to have a climate that makes it attractive for investment and, generally speaking, it has to give businesses the impression that they are welcome and that they are wanted and that the kind of long-term stability that comes from solid blue chip industries is something that makes our country an attractive one. This is one of the things that causes me great nervousness about the recent budget in Ontario, which is the height of irresponsibility, in my opinion. It seems to have been observed in that regard, indeed right around the globe one might say. So 1 think there is a role for government.
Finally, government has a responsibility to see that the infrastructure is there to make it possible for companies to do business coast to coast in this country. I am talking
about communications and transportation infrastructure. I find it intriguing to see members from Montreal expressing some concerns in this regard because, quite frankly, in Atlantic Canada we have a lot of reservations about the quality of the infrastructure and the transportation infrastructure that exists for our benefit vis-a-vis the apparent national interest in ensuring the viability of the port of Montreal and the transportation systems that serve Montreal. I find it intriguing that people from Montreal would have reservations about that when we in Atlantic Canada have probably been stifled more by this single fact than anything else throughout history since Confederation.
However, the debate today is not on Atlantic Canada, it is on Montreal. Montreal, in my judgment, has excellent prospects. Now, there is one big cloud on the horizon. Let us face it, nothing will discourage investment-and it is investment that leads to jobs, not just government spending-like a sense of political instability. That is the cloud in my judgment that is hanging over the head not only of Montreal, not only of Quebec, but indeed the whole of Canada.
I think all members of this House have to stand together in recognizing that the key to our future prosperity in Montreal, Quebec, Atlantic Canada- throughout Canada-lies in having a government that shows sound financial management and the courage and economic vision to lead this country into the 21st century. Also it should have the ability and the courage to reunify our country as we work toward a renewed confederation that will be caring and will value self-reliance among its citizens, a confederation that will show respect for the people of all regions, all linguistic groups, all races of this country. It must be a system of government that will show regional balance, will not pit one region against the other and will give all equal opportunity to participate: quite simply a Canada that has room for all Canadians.
That kind of Canada under the leadership this government has provided will not only lead to economic prosperity for that great city of Montreal, but indeed for all parts of Canada.

place I know personally. It is a place with a joie de vivre that one cannot help but be impressed by.

What we are talking about here is not expenditure in the sense of money which goes out and leaves nothing behind. When a large company makes such an investment, for instance, in a new factory, or a new port facility or something like that, new transportation items which it is going to utilize, we do not say to that company: "You're being wasteful. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I must say that I am very happy to take part in this debate, today. As a former businessman, I know Montreal, even if I come from a rural area, Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup.
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues described to you the strategies adopted by the government to develop the economic potential of the Montreal area. As for me, I would like to draw your attention on the measures taken by the government to develop international activities in Montreal.
The government believes that the development of international activities in Montreal is an excellent way to revitalize the regional economy. According to this logic, the government has decided to establish in Montreal the headquarters of the Canadian Space Agency to increase the stimulation of the existing potential, both in the related industrial activities and in the presence of Montreal in international networks.
Already, in 1986, the Picard Report had stressed that Montreal had the required qualifications to become an international city, including its bilingual and bicultural character. Montreal was at that time home for two prestigious international organizations, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Air Transport Association (IATA). Since then, it welcomed the International Society of Aeronautical Telecommunications (ISAT). Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the Picard Report mentioned a positive factor for Montreal, and that is Canada's membership in organizations such as the Commonwealth and La Francophonie, which has helped several companies reach out to the world.
Mr. Speaker, the Picard Report recommended that all levels of government recognize the importance of international organizations and facilitate their establishment in Montreal. The Canadian government recognized this objective and committed itself to making Montreal an important world centre which would have branches of governmental and non-governmental organizations dealing with international affairs, as well as to developing and promoting other international activities in Montreal. To this end, the government worked on devising incentives which would attract such organisations and facilitate their operations.
As a first step, the government, jointly with the Quebec government and the City of Montreal, is helping the Societe du centre de conferences internationales, a non-profit organization, to conduct studies on the feasibility of creating an international city and to make concrete proposals for the development of international activities in Montreal. The international city would bring together, under one roof, the ICAO headquarters, an international conference centre and other international activities or organizations.
Mr. Speaker, the government is waiting for a report on these studies before announcing a final decision about this project. The ICAO will decide on a possible move at its next plenary session in September 1992.
I would like to stress, Mr. Speaker, that the government signed last year an agreement with the ICAO in which we committed ourselves to providing better working conditions to this organization and its employees.
The federal government has recently contributed to the installation of three international organizations in Montreal. Last year, it created the International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development, which it put in Montreal and provided with a $15 million budget over 5 years. Under the direction of Mr. Ed Broadbent, whom hon. members know well, this organisation will contribute to the strengthening of democratic institutions and programs in the world by promoting research, sponsoring conferences and bringing technical assistance and financial help to local initiatives in the Third World.
It has also contributed $10 million to the establishment in Montreal of the permanent secretary of the Multilateral Fund of the Montreal Protocol on the Ozone Layer. This is the second United Nations organization, after the ICAO, to establish in Canada. It is an office composed of approximately twenty persons; its task is to administer an international fund which could grow to $240 millions in the next three years.
It also contributed financially to the establishment in Montreal of the head office of the International Centre of Films for Children and Young People (ICFCYP). This is an international association created under the United Nations auspices. It produces and distributes films which can promote a better understanding among nations.
June 4, 1991

As in the case of projects developed jointly by the private sector and the federal and other governments, the government supports a joint initiative of the Metropolitan Montreal Chamber of Commerce and the EDI Council of Canada. This initiative concerns the establishment of an office in Montreal for the realization of a program for the promotion and training on EDI and the management of activities pertaining to the creation of an EDI international agency. EDI is a process of electronic data exchange which helps firms to save a lot of money and to be more efficient and faster in their exchanges. In this matter, like England and the Netherlands, the government supports the development of these kinds of activities in Montreal. It helped establish a non-profit corporation, under a board of directors whose members are prominent in the trade and transportation sector in Montreal, including the Port of Montreal and shipping, railway and trucking companies, for the purpose of introducing an EDI system that will meet the needs of the transportation industry and related sectors. The results of this initiative will be an important part of the process of setting up the EDI Institute.
Although the list of federal initiatives in the international field in Montreal is a long one, there are four more measures I must mention:
First, support for establishing an institute for creativity and design research will promote, stimulate and enhance the development of skills Canadian and excellence of international calibre in various design disciplines.
Second, support for institutions specializing training such as the Telecommunications Executive Management Institute of Canada (TEMIC), established in Montreal in 1986. The institute has attracted over 200 managers from 70 countries who acquired telecommunications skills, thanks to co-operation between the private sector, including Bell Canada, Teleglobe, Northern Telecom, and the government.
Third, support for the International Aviation Management Training Institute (IAMTI) which after four years has 1,200 graduates in 120 countries.

Fourth, the patent legislation (Bill C-22) passed by Parliament to promote research and development in the pharmaceutical industry. As a result of this legislation, many pharmaceutical companies located in Montreal have started to expand their facilities.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that these examples have demonstrated the Canadian government's commitment to implementing a concrete policy for developing and promoting international activities in Montreal. In fact, the government is very much aware of the need to include both business, educational institutions, and international governmental and non-governmental organizations in these activities. Only by fostering joint action by both the private and public sectors, Mr. Speaker, can the government contribute to the long-term economic development in the Montreal area.
Today, Mr. Speaker, Montreal should be able to develop adequately its high-technology sector and to strengthen its traditional industry. The most frequent issues preventing Montreal from reaching these objectives without the govcrncment intervention arc, among others, the shortage of a highly skilled work force, the lack of investment in research and development, the absence of risk capital to start up small high-technology businesses and a weak partnership from universities, industries, financial institutions in particular. Various governments have already recognized the weaknesses of Montreal, particularly in the east and the south-west of the city, where special programs have been implemented. With my background as a businessman, I consider Montreal to be the heart and the engine of the economy of the province of Quebec.
