speechtext: Order, please. Resuming debate. The hon. member for Lachine-Lac-Saint-Louis.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join in this debate to discuss the economic development challenge in Montreal, and to join the other speakers who have recorded the concerns we all have for a full and equal share on the part of Montrealais in this economic recovery program.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace asks this government to create jobs in Montreal. Here is our response. Mr. Speaker, this government spent more than $32 million during the last year to do precisely that. Did my colleague mention it in his motion? I do not think so.
It bears repeating that between April 1, 1990 and March 31, 1991, this government spent more than $32 million, $32,076,850 to be specific, in order to create jobs in the city of Montreal, and 7,925 people benefitted from this help. Part of this money was used to protect jobs, which is more or less like creating new ones. If a job is at risk and the government steps in to protect it, it is like job creation.
[English ]
Work sharing is a godsend for a company that is staring disaster in the face and will have to lay off and thus lose valued skilled workers in order to survive. The work sharing program, by shortening the work week by one to three days, lets workers keep their jobs, thereby keeping up their skills.
I can speak from personal experience in the riding of Lachine that the work sharing program is working. With the aid of the Government of Canada two of our major corporations, Jenkins Incorporated and one other, have applied for and received the support they needed to keep those jobs alive.
Job creation, as any employer knows, always happens when there are workers around with the right skills or people with the ability to learn the job quickly and then relearn it when some new technology or method comes along that radically changes the nature of the job, rendering the old skills obsolete.

I am talking about people who can adjust, Mr. Speaker, people who can read, count and understand a manual or remember complex instructions, people who are part of today's culture and who can learn the required skills when they are needed. Those are the people who would really create jobs, people who can adjust. The 8,000 Montrealers or so who got help from the government last year all have skills or had to learn some in order to play an active role in the work force.
Those who had practically no useful skills were registered in a government job training program. Now, thanks to training funded by our government, those Montrealers are on their way to self-sufficiency again.

The training costs for about 100 unemployed, unskilled people anywhere in the country can run close to $1 million, or on a per capita basis roughly $8,500 to $10,000 per individual trainee. I mention this to point out how much it costs to properly train an unskilled, unemployed person for work. In fact, re-employment training is so expensive that it requires the involvement of many partners to make it viable.

June 4, 1991
Supply
The government funds skills training programs for the unemployed.
The government also wants to encourage employers to fund training and retraining for their workers who may be at risk or falling behind in productivity.
This morning in Lachine, I learned that there was a meeting of some 80 employers, industrial and commercial companies, with the school authority, together with the support of the Government of Canada, for the very purpose of organizing these very courses to bring those basic skills into the work place.
I am proud that there is this initiative, and I am sure it is being repeated and will be repeated right across the country. The government wants to encourage employers to fund training and retraining for their workers who may be at risk of falling behind in productivity.
That is why in the Speech from the Throne the government vowed to begin the effort now to quadruple the training provided by employers to their employees.
[ Translation ]
Our training programs help the unemployed to acquire basic and vocational skills which they need to find a job. Employers can also help their staff to keep their skills up to date and prevent them from loosing their job.

Survival skills include communication, mathematics and job search techniques, basic skills that you and I acquired long ago and now take for granted. Deprived of these basic skills, one is bound to lose his or her self-esteem. We have a particular example of this among the management and executive professional class in the west of Montreal.
There is a self-help program, Executives Available, which has put together the self-assistance and encouragement that allows those people who have been without work and losing confidence to come back into the work force with a new sense of confidence.
As all of us know, the loss of self-esteem usually cancels or depreciates one's ability and desire to compete in today's fast changing job market.
Basic training skills therefore start the unemployed person back on the road to recovery. That is why this training is so vital to our re-employment strategy. That is why re-employment training can cost $10,000 per trainee.
The re-learning of basic survival skills is often slow and time consuming, eating up training dollars before the occupational training takes place. It is why we made the unemployment insurance system more flexible and why we are using UI moneys to help claimants require skills through training and get back to work faster.
Our reform of the Unemployment Insurance Act, Bill C-21, so actively resisted by opposition members has become an integral part of our effort to create jobs through training. That is what Canadians say they want, work and not welfare.

Bill C-21 was generally perceived as a measure intended to change the rules governing benefits. That is only half the truth. The bill really contained provisions to eliminate certain factors likely to deter the unemployed to go back to work. It did justice to families whose parents are working, to older workers and others, by giving them access to unemployment benefits.

Equally important are measures that brought the UI program into line with the labour market of the 1990s, a labour market which is very different from the one that existed when UI was first set up.
The nature of and causes of unemployment today are very different from those of 10, 20 and 30 years ago. At one time, temporary passive income support made sense for someone out of work because unemployment was something they could simply wait out.
Today, that passive approach can easily be a ticket to permanent unemployment.
Today people are out of work even when jobs are available because their skills just do not match the demands of the marketplace. No amount of waiting will change that.
If UI is to continue to function effectively as a safety net, people need to be able to use it more constructively as a tool for re-employment through training and counselling that will help them re-enter a changing workplace.

The Labour Force Development Strategy announced in 1989 is a strategy that places a major emphasis on skills development, counselling and employment training. It designates some $550 million a year for 60,000 UI recipients who previously were not eligible for job training.
The LFDS is an internationally proven formula for strengthening a country's labour force and contains measures geared specifically to help communities such as the one the hon. member represents. These measures include strengthening the Community Futures Program and the Industrial Adjustment Service.
Both programs are receiving additional funding under LFDS. Community Futures Program will see its 1991 budget increased from $50 million to $198 million, while Industrial Adjustment Service's allocation is being doubled from $15 million to $30 million.
These programs cost a lot of money but in human terms, skills training for the unemployed appears on the credit side of any social ledger, yielding benefits not in dollars, but in human achievement.

If it were possible to represent the well-being using a balance sheet, the lack of retraining would surely appear under the liabilities, because it results in prolonged unemployment, in lost productivity, in increasing dissatisfaction, and in the wasting of human resources.
That is a terrible perspective for our fragile economy, which is already undermined by the shortages of manpower and by the very limited training possibilities offered by the private sector.

We must improve the climate of the labour market by building a stronger learning culture and providing more training opportunities for those who need it most. The training of workers helps Canada's economy by easing skills shortages. Training the unemployed offsets the costly side effects of unemployment, such as crime, disease, substance abuse and family and mental breakdown.
With respect to training workers, Canada needs a training compact between workers and employers. The private sector knows better than government where and how training should be provided and yet formal training is currently offered by only one quarter of Canada's businesses.

Mr. Speaker, that is why we have devoted more money to vocational training and development than any other

Canadian government before us. We did so when we became aware of the difficult economic climate in the world.

I am confident that the training and adjustment programs this government is delivering in Montreal and across the country will be of long-term benefit to Montrealers and Canadians.

Mr. Guy H. Arseneault (Restigouche-Chaleur)
moves:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of sending a petition to Her Majesty the Queen for a grant of arms to amend the motto on the Coat of Arms of Canada to read: A Man usque act Mare usque ad Marc.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for letting me the first one to discuss the motion that I have moved.
Before starting my speech, I would like to bring to your attention a spelling mistake in the wording of the motion in the Order Paper, as well as in the Projected Order of Business. Indeed, in the new motto that I propose A Mari usque ad Mare usque ad Mare, the second and third "Mare" should be spelled M-A-R-E and not M-A-R-I.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, the coat of arms of Canada bear the motto A Mari usque ad Mare, which symbolizes the vastness of our country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Since its adoption in 1921, this motto has been a reminder to all Canadians that the vastness of their country is truly remarkable and that even if our country is so large, it is united through a single and unique nation called Canada.
June 4. 1991

However, if this motto was meant to establish a symbolic link between all Canadians, and if it was meant to be a reflection of our geography, it nevertheless as one serious flaw, in that it ignores the geography and the residents of the North.
[English\
What I want to do today is give some background information on the motto, my reasons for presenting this motion and a few other supporting points.
The first official use came in 1906 when the phrase was engraved on the head of the mace of the legislative assembly of the new province of Saskatchewan. At that time Under-Secretary of State Joseph Pope became familiar with the future motto and took a liking to it.
In 1919 Pope was named to a committee appointed by the federal government to recommend a new design for the arms of Canada. Although no motto was included on the old shield, one was to be included in the new arms. The coat of arms and the motto were approved by Order in Council on April 21, 1921, and by Royal proclamation on November 21, 1921.
The territorial evolution of Canada helps us to understand the origins of the motto and, let us hope, will provide a harbinger of a new motto. Obviously the present motto reflects an east-west bias which tends to ignore Canada's north. However, an overview of the territorial evolution of the north reveals that continual changes were made to boundaries before 1912 and may help explain why a more accurate motto was not devised sooner.
Given the state of flux of the boundaries and the area's relative state of isolation and sparse population, it probably was not politically expedient to adopt the motto which is truly reflective of our country's history and geography.
The coat of arms and the motto recognize Canada's evolution to a certain point. The shield of the coat of arms displays the arms of England, Scotland, Ireland and France and to symbolize the nation's founding races, underneath the four quarters on a white field is a sprig of three maple leafs to indicate the new nation of many peoples.
Private Members' Business
There is one very noticeable exception, the first nations. Neither the shield nor the motto directly refer to them. Why not accept the motion proposed as a sign of recognition of Canada's first nations.
You may say that sums up in a nutshell why we should accept this motion, but I want to explain why I presented the motion in particular. My background as a teacher of Canadian history in the secondary school system in the province of New Brunswick has given me an insight into some of the problems we face here in Canada.
I also have an aboriginal population in my riding and there are a number of native reserves throughout New Brunswick. I have had the occasion of meeting with those groups time and time again.
In my background as a history teacher I have come to the conclusion that, and in many discussions in class with students from my region, from the riding of Resti-gouche-Chaleur, it has also been pointed out, it seemed to be an oversight. We have a coat of arms, a Canadian motto that says from sea to sea only.
Basically, it was meetings in the classroom, meetings with native groups in New Brunswick, in my riding more specifically, that brought this to a point. As a history teacher I didn't expect to be a member of Parliament some day and be in a position to maybe influence the changing of this motto, but here I am. That is one of the promises that I made to myself. If ever I got into a position to be able to influence such a change, then I would bring it up. This is why I have decided to present this motion today.
With regard to the changing of the motto, since becoming a member of Parliament I have noticed that the Prime Minister of Canada, the right hon. Brian Mulroney, has made a number of speeches in the House where he has, and rightly so, a number of times referred to the phrase: "from coast to coast to coast", again re-emphasizing the current use.
I have noticed the Leader of the Opposition has used it and the leader of the third party has used it. I have noticed that it has become common practice for ministers of the Crown to use it. What I am trying to do today is perhaps make it legal to a certain extent. In some respects it could be seen as a matter of housekeeping.

June 4, 1991
Private Members' Business
I think it is more important than that. The implementation of this new motto would send a positive message to northern residents at little or no cost to the federal government, and would help foster national unity. When we look at the question of national unity, specifically the question of the aboriginals, the question of aboriginals in respect to last summer even, we know that they have many problems which have never been addressed properly. It would at least be a gesture of good faith to approve this change in the motto.
I believe that it would also be a psychological link, a symbol similar to some of the symbols we have had in the past, symbols such as John A. Macdonald's national policy. The Broadcast Act for a while talked about Canadian unity, so there was that linkage. There is the Official Languages Act and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. These have all become very important symbolic and psychological links binding Canadians from all regions.
I would hope that acceptance of this motion would be considered as very important, would be considered as sending a message to the north that: "You are part of this great country". We want that fact to be legally recognized.
It has certainly become common practice for members in their speeches to use "from sea to sea to sea" or "from coast to coast to coast". I would hope that the members on the other side and the members of the third party would see fit to recognize that.
I would say, because of its common use and because of the influence of the north now, our great country, that it would certainly be unacceptable to keep the status quo. We should recognize the geographical reality of the north, as well as the members of our first nations and other northern residents. In fact, if we were not to recognize this fact it might send a negative message to them.
I think it is very important that we do recognize that a change in our motto is necessary.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the adoption of a new motto would obviously be perceived as
a recognition of the importance of the Canadian North and of the First Nations, as well as of all the residents of that region. I believe that the government should spare no efforts to give to Canadians a motto that is a true reflection of the country and of its regions.
At a time when Canada faces a serious identity crisis, this initiative could help in a significant way to preserve national unity. A Mari Usque Ad Mare Usque Ad Mare.

[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Inuktitut.]

Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure to speak to this motion put forward by my hon. colleague. I think it is something that needs to be recognized within this House of Commons and within this great country.
Very often the people today in this House, as my colleague stated earlier, have been saying "from coast to coast to coast"-whether it is the right hon. Prime Minister or other members of his government or our illustrious Leader of the Official Opposition or the Leader of the New Democratic Party. So, I think it is incumbent upon all members of this House to use either "from sea to sea to sea" or "coast to coast to coast" because it has to be recognized that Canada is surrounded by three oceans-the Pacific Ocean, the Arctic Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean, of which the Arctic coast has the longest shoreline. Surely that alone should be enough to make people realize that there are three coasts to recognize.
Often when I am listening or watching CBC Radio or CBC Television I get bothered when the commentator says: "from coast to coast". I always want to phone and remind them that they have to mention the third coast. Now, it may very well be that they are talking about the Atlantic coast and the Arctic coast, or the Pacific coast and the Arctic coast, but I think it would be even better if they said: "coast to coast to coast".
When "from sea to sea" was first used it may have indeed been accurate, but it is no longer. In 1898 Yukon was carved out of the Northwest Territories. After the creation of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in 1905, the present boundaries of the Northwest Territo-
June 4, 1991

ries were finalized. So it was not until 1905 that we could start using "coast to coast to coast".
Canada's Arctic territory is second only in size to that of the U.S.S.R. Together, Yukon and the Northwest Territories comprise 40 per cent of the area of Canada. Almost half of the population of Canada's northern region are aboriginal people, and more in the Northwest Territories where roughly 50 per cent in the Western Arctic and about 85 per cent in the Eastern Arctic are aboriginal people, and fewer in the Yukon.
When my colleague was talking about the founding nations, the first nations, he was indeed right in saying that the area that is occupied by the majority of aboriginal people-in this case the Northwest Territories- should be recognized as a very real part of Canada. The north is unique and everybody has to recognize this. It is a unique and distinct region of Canada, politically, socially, culturally and economically.
It is always offensive to those of us who come from the north when we are forgotten in Canada's national symbols. In this case again it may have been accurate back in 1898 to say "coast to coast", but it is not the case any more. Therefore, we should be recognized as part of the great country of Canada.
As well as my colleague from the Western Arctic, I am constantly trying to remind members of this House of Commons and the rest of Canada about the existence of the north, of the Inuit, the Dene or other people who occupy the Northwest Territories as well as Yukon.
Canada's north has always occupied a strategic military position. Northerners and particularly aboriginal people, by virtue of their residency in the north, have proved and sustained Canada's sovereignty in the Arctic. Recently the significance of Arctic and global environmental issues have been recognized.
Over the past few years scientific, social, cultural and political exchanges have multiplied between Canada's northern territories and other circumpolar nations. A circumpolar environmental protection agreement will be signed in Finland later this month.
The circumpolar dimension of Canada's foreign policy is becoming increasingly important. It is extremely important that Canada's symbols recognize all of Canada's
Private Members' Business
component parts and peoples. The northern territories and the Arctic Ocean are integral parts of Canada; the northern residents are a very real part of Canada and consider themselves very Canadian. We deserve to be acknowledged in this great country.
It is time to change our motto. It is appropriate at this important stage of Canadian constitutional renewal to embrace all parts of this country and all Canadians. Supporting the motion of my hon. colleague would be a significant national reconciliation initiative by this federal Parliament.
This is not a partisan issue. What is under discussion here is the recognition of a simple geographic and political fact as well as a symbolic one.
I ask hon. members on all sides to support this motion and to recognize the north and the Arctic Ocean, and I urge the House to acknowledge that Canada stretches from sea to sea to sea.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I rise in this afternoon's debate on Motion No. 387, a motion by our hon. colleague for Restigouche which asks this House to affirm its intention to alter the motto of the Coat of Arms of Canada from A Mari usque ad Mare to A Mari usque ad Mare usque ad Mare.
First of all I want to thank the member for Restigouche for bringing to my attention the coat of arms, which perhaps I had not recognized as often as I should. Now that I have become involved with this, I see it on your chair, on our money, on our letterheads and almost everywhere we look here. I do compliment the member for that and thank him.
I view this debate as an opportunity, not only to discuss the merits of my hon. colleague's proposal, but also an opportunity for the House early in a new session of Parliament where the very future of Canada will be shaped to discuss the symbols of the country, the symbols which are common to all Canadians.
Let me turn specifically to the motion. Our colleague would wish to alter the motto of Canada. Our colleague would wish to alter that motto to reflect our geographic reality, the reality of which every member in this House is justifiably proud. This great land of ours runs from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from the 49th parallel to the

June 4, 1991
Private Members' Business
North Pole, and the waters of three of the world's great oceans wash on our shores.
There are very few nations in the world, very few, that can claim the geographic bounty and beauty of Canada. There are very few nations that can claim the richness brought on by the very size of the land mass of our Canada. There are even fewer nations that can claim the richness of a population whose origins stem from virtually every corner of the globe.
Canada is truly a blessed land. Those who would say we are not, the nay sayers who say this country should be torn asunder fail to acknowledge the bounty, the richness, the prosperity and the promise that has been, that is and that will be our Canada.
Our hon. colleague from Restigouche asked us to change a motto which we have had formally since November 21, 1921. Those words in English, "from sea to sea", are inextricably linked.
Not only is the motto of Canada on our coat of arms, it is also linked to the vision of the Fathers of Confederation in the 1860s.
We take for granted many things about our country. That seems to be a characteristic of the way we see ourselves. We do have a motto. It is "from sea to sea", but do we know its roots? We must understand that it is not a statement of just geography but a statement of promise and hope.
The motto which we celebrate is not just a series of words. The motto "from sea to sea" is derived from the 72nd Psalm, A Song for Solomon.
Something else is derived from that 72nd Psalm, and is the very title of our country. We are the Dominion of Canada and when the Fathers of Confederation were grappling with what to call the very first British colonies to achieve true, responsible self-determination, there were many problems.
Some wished to call it the kingdom of Canada. Others did not know what we should be called, but clearly not "a republic" or "a kingdom".
In those days inspiration was found in Psalm 72. I will read from it: "He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth."
The 72nd Psalm speaks about the righteousness of rulers and Divine Province's guidance of rulers. The
72nd Psalm speaks about the beauty of the earth, its majesty, its wealth and how it sustains us.
Let me quote from the third verse: "The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills, by righteousness." The 72nd Psalm speaks of hope of a people in other lands.
When my hon. colleague wishes to change our motto on the crest of our coat of arms by adding a third "sea" in order to express a geographic reality, he is proposing to not only alter words, but to alter the deep-seated thoughts and principles.
He proposes to alter the very idea of our name and of our title as a land.
There is a very clear relationship between our title, the Dominion of Canada, and the motto "from sea to sea". We should not alter it. I find it particularly apt that the Fathers of Confederation would have gone to the 72nd Psalm.
In 1867, we were a land of just one sea. We were a small country. We were made up of four, small, isolated colonies huddling on the North American land mass confronting a powerful neighbour, the United States of America in its most expansionist era.
Canada was made up of four small colonies without even a railroad linking them; four colonies which stopped at what is today Thunder Bay; four colonies which were 200 or 300 miles from the St. Lawrence watershed.
Yet the promise and hope of the Fathers of Confederation, Macdonald, Cartier and Tupper was the future of Canada. Those leaders, from the day of Confederation, strove without rest to shape what I proudly say is the world's greatest country.
Those leaders dared to think larger. Those leaders, within three years, dared to acquire responsibility for virtually all of what would become the land mass of Canada. From four isolated colonies our Fathers of Confederation dared to shape Canada.
I know that there are many in society today who think that history is bunk. I certainly do not believe that. I do not believe a people can know where they wish to go until they know where they have been.
I think we need to know more about the symbols of Canada. I think we need to know more about the things which tie us together. We should not think of them
June 4, 1991

merely as conveniences, as a trademark or as a commercial brand name that we can change from time to time.
Our coat of arms, our motto, is not a brand name. It is not a commercial logo. It is one of the proudest symbols of one of the world's proudest countries.
My hon. colleague from Restigouche feels that we must reflect the north of our country, and I respect that but we must reflect our diversity. We do not extend just from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Our country is larger than that, but our motto is not derived from a mere Latin Translation of a geography. It is derived from a biblical text which speaks about a people and their aspirations.
That is why I feel it is not a simple matter of changing a few words. I am not even going to discuss the costs in doing that, but there are obvious costs.
I do not feel comfortable in supporting the motion of my colleague from Restigouche. I think he has missed the mark about what this motto is about and what Canadian symbols are about.
These are difficult times in Canada. We need to look back and look forward at the same time, to benefit and build on what we do the best and to rectify that which may have kept us apart.
I think symbols like our flag, our motto, our coat of arms and our basic parliamentary system of government are things which are special to all Canadians and I do not think we should tinker with them on the spur of the moment. We should think very seriously about their origins and their meaning before we do anything to change our symbols. I know this proposal to change the motto has been made before. I have heard leaders from our north make similar statements and I really understand and appreciate their concerns. They think that too many Canadians only think in terms of that narrow band where most of us live, which runs east to west.
That may be so in some instances but there are so many other ways to recognize the importance of the north; to recognize the majesty, the grandeur of all of Canada, its riches and prosperity. Our motto is not a statement of geography alone. It is a statement of commitment and what our hon. friend from Restigouche proposes would mean changing for the wrong reason that statement of promising commitment.
Private Members' Business
It has been a great pleasure this afternoon to participate in this debate on an important symbol of Canada and I only hope that the spirit of co-operation and fair debate that we are seeing will transfer into our work this autumn on reshaping our Canadian federation for the next century.
I think we are like the Fathers of Confederation. We are our heirs Parents of Confederation. The challenge of the past is handed to us. It is now for us to take up the torch and to shape the Canada for our children and for our children's children.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of Multicul-turalism and Citizenship):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for allowing me to take part in the debate today on the motion of the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur in which he asks the House to change the Canadian motto which is now "from sea to sea" to "from sea to sea to sea".
Mr. Speaker, I have here the Projected Order of Business for today and I read motion M-387. Being of Italian origin, I would like to correct a small error that has been bothering me and, unless I am mistaken, that would improve the Latin version. You will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, as you are well informed in this matter, it is: ad Mare and not ad Mari. I would appreciate to see the correction. It should read: ad Mare ad Mare and not ad Mari, unless my colleague has made the correction, because it is difficult to pick up visually. Mare also comes both from Latin and Italian, it is the same. We all know it translates the word ocean.
So, thank you, Mr. Speaker, I find the whole thing perfectly acceptable if the member has made the correction, but I might have missed this part of his speech.
Mr. Speaker, it seems appropriate, at the beginning of this new session of Parliament, to have the opportunity to debate a motion concerning such a fundamental point in a country as its motto.
During the last few weeks, my colleague the right hon. member for Yellowhead, who was here a few minutes ago, has been criss-crossing the country to try to establish a consensus among its citizens and its leaders, a consensus on the need to build a new Canada, a Canada

June 4, 1991
Private Members' Business
of the 21th century, a Canada corresponding to the demands and aspirations of today's generation.
Mr. Speaker, 125 years ago, the Fathers of Confederation were almost in the same situation thus we are now. They were the leaders of four little colonies of British North America, four little colonies who banded together because they realized that this way, they could prosper, develop and build the society they were dreaming of. We are facing the same challenges today, Mr. Speaker. We must get together in order to shape our country for tomorrow. We must get together to shape a country united, strong and free. Mr. Speaker, what our hon. colleague for Restigouche-Chaleur wants is to change something that is fundamental to our country since we became the Dominion of Canada.
The motto of our country and its name come from the seventy-second psalm, the psalm of Salomon. They are taken from the eight verse that says: "He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth". Mr. Speaker, that verse is so full of promises and hope.
"Dominion", Mr. Speaker, is such a noble word. Through its roots, it brings us dignity and legitimacy. In that verse, we see all the great hopes the Fathers of Confederation shared. To them, the phrase "from sea to sea" was a metaphor for their dreams and their hopes, not only a geographic description.
They had settled along the Atlantic coast and on both sides of the St. Lawrence River. However, Mr. Speaker, the Fathers of Confederation dreamt of a country extending from coast to coast and lived in the land of the Great River. They wanted a country that stretched to the furthest shores.
Such was, Mr. Speaker, the challenge facing the Fathers of Confederation: to give shape to a huge country in the northern part of this continent.
I do not think that we should change our motto simply because this huge country of ours has three oceans off its shores instead of two. This is not the place to discuss such trivial issues, nor is this is the way to go about it.
What we are talking about here, Mr. Speaker, is the reason why we, in this House, would want to change the
motto of this great country, the reason why we would want to change our Coat of Arms.
This brings me to raise a very important question in the context of today's debate. Our motto is neither a brand name nor a slogan a cereal company tested on consumers. Our motto reflects the image we have of ourselves. Our Coat of Arms reflects who we are and where we come from. Let me tell you a few things about the Coat of Arms of Canada, Mr. Speaker. We do not have to go out of this Chamber to look at it. It is all around us. There is even one right above your head. It is everywhere in this room.
Some argue that our Coat of Arms is outdated, a survival from the past. I disagree. I think that our Coat of Arms is as current today as it was on that day, in November 1921, when the late King George V proclaimed the Coat of Arms of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, our Coat of Arms shows our main roots. There is the fleur-de-lis from France, the royal heart from Ireland, the unicorn from Scotland, the lion from England and, in a conspicuous place, three maples leaves on a white field. Only a few Canadians probably know that when our Coat of Arms was proclaimed in 1921, red and white were proclaimed to be the colours of Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me extremely accurate and appropriate that the flag of our great country, our Maple Leaf, be red and white. Those are our historical colours, the colours of Canada.
I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, that all Canadians understand the origin of our motto and what inspired it. I am not sure either that they understand the symbolic nature of our flag.
That is rather disturbing. When I go to the United States, I am immediately amazed at how Americans, young and old, readily understand the symbols of then-great republic. Almost everyone understand their motto E Pluribus Unum-Out of many, one. Most of them could tell you the story of Betsy Ross, and of the designing of their beautiful star-spangled banner.
Mr. Speaker, Americans do know about E pluribus unum. In Canada, it seems that we have been somewhat reluctant to instill in our children and citizens a deep understanding and appreciation of Canada and a sense of patriotism.
June 4. 1991

Mr. Speaker, I do not think we should change our fundamental symbols without giving the matter proper consideration. Before we change them, we should first learn to know them.
Mr. Speaker, we did not get a truly Canadian flag until 1965. The quest for a Canadian flag started in 1925, 40 years before we finally got our Hag. In 1946, the hon. Paul Martin, was Secretary of State when the first bill on Canadian citizenship making us real Canadian citizens was presented. Mr. Martin, whose son sits in front of me, promised a Canadian flag and a national anthem. But we had to wait 20 more years to have a flag that would be really ours.
Mr. Speaker, we now have all of that, a flag, a national anthem, our Canadian citizenship, a Coat of Arms and a motto. All members of this House are proud of those symbols. I am not at all convinced that the time has come for us to change something as fundamental as our motto.
Mr. Speaker, I know that I have only one minute left. I will try to be brief. I know that many people have proposed a new motto, "from coast to coast to coast", to reflect Canada's geographic reality. Northerners think that our motto does not take into account their beautiful Arctic Ocean. There are many other ways, besides changing our proud motto on the Coat of Arms of Canada, to recognize the geographic majesty of this country of ours, to make Canadians better understand what we have in common, what keeps us together. We are all proud, Mr. Speaker, of our Coat of Arms and, above all, we are proud to be Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for the opportunity to speak to the private member's bill brought forward by my colleague from Restigouche to have the coat of arms changed.
I see this particular private member's bill as one being very useful and very valuable in bringing to the Canadian conscience the fact that there is a third sea and that sea is one that is actualized by the people that live there and the diversity that exists there. It is recognition that the north is a growing, viable, political, constitutional entity, that it is not just an extension of the federal government of Canada. It is not just an extension that could be considered a colony and a distant land in the years
Private Members' Business
leading to the year 2000; it is in fact an area of Canada that is to be admired for its very difficult climate at times, but also for its diversity and the people who live there.
In reference to my hon. colleague from Restigouche's private member's bill, the change would be stated as sea, to sea, to sea, or, as many others would put it, coast to coast to coast. If you include the third coast, you are doing what we want to do in Canada these days, which is to express equality and inclusiveness in our efforts to bring this country together.
We are not excluded. It is known that Her Majesty has been to that sea and visited the people in the early 1970s.
I am sure that when the petition is brought to Her Majesty, she will recognize the viability of this particular private member's bill and because she has been there and shaken hands and looked into the faces of these people, she will know that this is something that needs to be done.
This particular coat of arms has not been in existence since the beginning of Confederation but only since 1921. Had we not taken the steps to change the previous flag, we would still be in a rather static state of having the old flag. But we endured a tremendous amount of debate and friction and we now have the new maple leaf Canada flag, which is something of which we are very proud.
In fact, there is room for improvement, there is room for change and I do not see why not.
In 1974 I went as a young person to that particular sea. I went as a young person with three children. I went to teach in the community of Tuktoyaktut which is a predominantly Inuvialuit community. I thought I would never see the sun again. It was the longest winter of my life but I learned to love that land. Every day, that I taught in that school I looked out the window and what did I see? I saw the Arctic Ocean from my classroom. In the fall, what did I see? I saw the beluga whale when I was standing on top of a Bombardier with my three children. I could see the beluga whale swimming in that see.
What did I see in the early seventies? I saw the first ship pull into the Beaufort Sea for Dome Petroleum, which created a great amount of activity. What else did I see? I experienced in that community on the third sea the first Inuit circumpolar meeting in that area which was attended by many prominent Canadians, including Justice Berger. It was there in 1974 that, in my aboriginal

June 4, 1991
Private Members' Business
language, I made my presentation on the Mackenzie Valley pipeline hearings to Mr. Berger.
The third sea is a reality to me. It is not a distant land. It is not a foreign colony. It is not something that I just talk about or read about in purple prose. It has the leadership.
We also have the Inuvialuit who settled their land claims. The Inuvialuit land claims agreement has allowed those people a certain amount of autonomy. It has allowed them to build institutions for the future. It has allowed them the opportunities for investment. It has allowed them some degree of autonomy with regard to the land they operate on and the kind of activities they engage in.
Mr. Speaker, if you look at that land and see it every day, this motion is not just changing a particular motto. It is reflecting in the symbols of this country a reality. What are symbols for? Symbols are to reflect and represent something that is true, something that represents this country, like the Constitution.
I have said many times that the Constitution is like a mirror. If we look into it we should be able to see ourselves. If we look at the symbols of our country, including this particular motto, and see "sea to sea", we do not just see the word "sea" but the reality of those people who live there, the people who have stood on those shores, the traders and the whalers who came there decades ago, centuries ago and mixed with the aboriginal people who live there, who worked and lived with those people and traded with those people and knew that particular sea.
It is not just a word. It is in fact a reality. It is something more than just words on a piece of paper. The symbolism placed on things that represent Canada, our country, are important for all of its people.
We have to look at a renewal. We talk about restructuring federalism. If we can restructure federalism why can we not restructure the symbols of this country? This is one of them.
Have those who oppose changing this motto stood on the shores of that sea? Have they shaken the hands of those people as Her Majesty has done herself, as the governor generals of the past have also done? That
brings a completely different perspective to the whole thing.
I spent three years of my working life in that community on the shores of that sea with those people. I watched the beluga whales swimming in that particular place. I watched the harvesting of the beluga by the Inuvialuit people. I taught their children. I know their culture and I know their reality and the pride they have in belonging to this country.
What about Arctic sovereignty? We talk about it as if it is a concept. It was a reality for the high Arctic exiles. Those are the people that were relocated from Kuujjuaq up to Grise Fiord to maintain Arctic sovereignty. This is the debate that is much disputed on the shores of the seas. Think of the polar expedition and where it goes. It crosses that sea. That is the reality.
When you think about Canada, you perhaps think about the area below the 49th parallel.
Well, the reality for those of us who live in the north is that we recognize that sea, we recognize the reality of that sea. We who are from the north feel that we are off the national grid when it comes to transportation, when it comes to many forms of communications and when it comes to the constitutional grid. We have to beg for a place at the table, for constitutional consultation.
However, if we do take a conscious step, as my colleague has, to make the difference, to say that the symbols of Canada are inclusive, that they are not exclusive, they do not alienate, they do not isolate, they include people. The people of that third sea need that recognition. It is the recognition of the north and recognition of the people who are there.
If laws were made not to be changed we would not be here. This is part of what we do. That is the reality of our lot in life. We amend laws because with the changing of time we need to do that, with the changing of needs we need to do that. That is the reality of what we do.
I hope it would be to the benefit of all. We live in a shrinking world which has to express and accommodate the cultural diversity of different peoples. This is the reality of Canada. We have many peoples, we have a beautiful country that is worth preserving.

June 4, 1991

I have travelled almost every part of this country and when I go home, when I fly over the delta which is part of my constituency, it is an overwhelming feeling that I have for my people and for that land. It is the love of the land which is inextricably intertwined with who we are. That is the way the people on the third sea live and realize their goals and aspirations.
I pay tribute to those people. They have lived under the most adverse climate throughout the years. They have had aspirations like every other Canadian. However, it is more expensive to live in the north. If we can change one symbol to reflect a reality, a beautiful reality, then we will be doing something to unite this country.
Mr. Speaker, if you would allow me, I would like unanimous consent to have the question now put to this particular private member's bill.
